ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necrosis (AVN):
What & why
📷 Image placeholder — Femoral head blood supply — retrograde retinacular vessels from the medial circumflex femoral artery, showing why an intracapsular neck fracture interrupts it and causes AVN.
Avascular necrosis (AVN), also called osteonecrosis, = death of bone tissue secondary to loss of its blood supply → bone destruction and loss of joint function.
The core concept: bone is living tissue that depends on a blood supply — interrupt it (steroids, alcohol, trauma…) and the bone infarcts, dies and collapses, destroying the overlying joint. The classic and commonest site is the femoral head (hip), because its blood supply is precarious — largely retrograde via the medial circumflex femoral artery — and easily disrupted. The clinical challenge: it is initially silent and X-ray-negative, so the priorities are to think of it in the at-risk patient (steroids, alcohol, a fractured hip) with new joint pain, image early with MRI (detects it before X-ray changes), and intervene before the joint collapses — after which joint replacement is the endpoint.
  • Commonest site = hip (femoral head).
  • Other sites have similarly tenuous blood supply: femoral condyles (knee), humeral head, scaphoid, talus.
The decisive fork: what caused it?
Identifying the cause guides prevention and management. The key causes:
CauseNote
Long-term steroid usethe commonest atraumatic cause (high-dose / prolonged corticosteroids)
Alcohol excessthe other leading atraumatic cause
Traumadisplaced femoral neck fracture / hip dislocation disrupting the femoral head's blood supply
Chemotherapya recognised precipitant
Other causes (mnemonic "ASEPTIC"): Alcohol / APS & SLE, Sickle cell disease (vaso-occlusion) / Steroids, the bEnds (decompression sickness / caisson disease), Pancreatitis, Trauma / radiation, Idiopathic, Caisson / Gaucher's disease.
High-yield rules: the two commonest atraumatic causes are STEROIDS + ALCOHOL; the commonest traumatic cause is a displaced femoral neck fracture / hip dislocation. This is why a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture (high AVN risk) is treated with replacement (hemiarthroplasty / THR) rather than fixation in older patients.
Clinical features
  • Initially asymptomatic — the early phase (before collapse) is silent.
  • Then pain in the affected joint: for the hip, groin / hip pain that is worse on weight-bearing and movement, may radiate, and is progressive.
  • Later: reduced range of movement, limp and joint stiffness as the bone collapses and secondary osteoarthritis develops.
The rule (high-yield): an at-risk patient (steroids / alcohol / prior hip fracture) with new, progressive, insidious hip or groin pain = AVN until proven otherwise — image early, before X-ray changes.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Side-by-side: normal/subtle early X-ray with crescent sign vs MRI showing early osteonecrosis — MRI detects AVN before X-ray changes.
Plain X-ray
  • May be NORMAL initially — a crucial point (early AVN is X-ray-negative).
  • Later: sclerosis and irregular articular surface of the femoral head; subchondral fracture and flattening, with the affected head appearing smaller than the other side.
  • Classic sign: the "crescent sign" — a subchondral lucency indicating subchondral collapse.
MRI = gold standard
  • The most sensitive test — detects AVN early, before X-ray changes appear, allowing joint-preserving intervention.
Staging: AVN is staged (e.g. Ficat classification) on X-ray / MRI findings — this guides whether to attempt joint preservation or proceed to replacement.
The rule (high-yield): X-ray may be normal early → if AVN is suspected, get an MRI (gold standard, detects it early).
Management
Overarching principle: early / pre-collapse → joint-preserving measures; late / collapsed joint → joint replacement; and always address the underlying cause.
Address the cause + early (pre-collapse)
  • Reduce / stop steroids where possible, reduce alcohol, manage the precipitant.
  • Protected weight-bearing + analgesia.
  • Core decompression — drilling the necrotic segment to relieve pressure and promote revascularisation, ± bone grafting — for early disease before collapse.
  • Bisphosphonates may slow progression (limited evidence).
Late (collapsed / advanced)
  • Joint replacement — total hip replacement (THR) is the definitive treatment for a collapsed femoral head / secondary osteoarthritis.
The staging principle (high-yield): pre-collapse → joint-preserving (core decompression); post-collapse → joint replacement. Hence the value of early MRI diagnosis — to catch it before collapse.
Exam pearls
What it is
Death of bone from loss of blood supply → bone collapse + joint destruction; commonest site = femoral head (hip), which has a precarious retrograde blood supply.
Causes
Commonest atraumatic = long-term STEROIDS + ALCOHOL; commonest traumatic = displaced femoral neck fracture / hip dislocation; also chemo, sickle cell, SLE/APS, the bends, Gaucher's, radiation, idiopathic.
Features
Initially asymptomatic → progressive groin/hip pain (worse on weight-bearing) → later stiffness + reduced ROM.
X-ray
May be NORMAL early; later sclerosis, irregular articular surface, subchondral fracture/flattening, "crescent sign".
MRI = gold standard
Most sensitive; detects AVN before X-ray changes → enables joint-preserving treatment.
Management
Treat the cause; early/pre-collapse → joint-preserving (core decompression); late/collapsed → joint replacement (THR). Displaced femoral neck fracture = high AVN risk → replacement, not fixation, in older patients.
ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst:
What & why
📷 Image placeholder — Posterior knee anatomy showing synovial fluid distending the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa in the popliteal fossa, communicating with the knee joint.
Baker's cyst (popliteal cyst) = a fluid-filled swelling behind the knee — not a true cyst, but a distension of the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa.
The core concept: synovial fluid from the knee joint accumulates in (or communicates with) the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa in the popliteal fossa — essentially fluid bulging out at the back of the knee. Two clinical priorities: (1) distinguish primary (benign, children) from secondary (a marker of underlying joint pathology, adults); and (2) — most importantly — recognise that a RUPTURED cyst mimics a DVT (calf pain/swelling), making it a key DVT differential. Most are benign and asymptomatic; in adults, management targets the underlying cause.
  • Named after the surgeon William Baker; common; usually benign.
The decisive fork: primary vs secondary
The first clinical question — is it benign (primary) or a sign of joint disease (secondary)?
PrimarySecondary
Causeno underlying pathologyan underlying condition (e.g. osteoarthritis)
Ageusually childrenusually adults
Significancebenignmarker of intra-articular knee pathology
Associationsnoneosteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, meniscal tears, gout
The rule (high-yield): primary = no underlying pathology, in children (benign); secondary = due to an underlying condition (e.g. osteoarthritis), in adults. In an adult, a Baker's cyst signals knee joint pathology — look for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis or a meniscal tear.
The child point: a child with an asymptomatic, fluctuant swelling behind the knee = likely a Baker's cyst — benign, needs no treatment.
Clinical features
  • Swelling in the popliteal fossa (behind the knee) — often fluctuant, more prominent on standing / knee extension and softening or disappearing on flexion ("Foucher's sign").
  • May be asymptomatic, or cause posterior knee discomfort/tightness, a mass sensation, or restricted flexion.
The rule (high-yield): a fluctuant swelling in the popliteal fossa behind the knee = Baker's cyst.
The decisive fork: ruptured cyst vs DVT
📷 Image placeholder — Ruptured Baker's cyst with pseudothrombophlebitis — acute calf pain/swelling and the crescent sign (ecchymosis around the ankle); exclude DVT before attributing to cyst rupture.
The most important point: if the cyst RUPTURES, it produces symptoms similar to a DVT — pain, redness and swelling in the calf.
Ruptured Baker's cystDVT
Presentationacute calf pain / swelling / rednesscalf pain / swelling / redness
Clueoften a history of a popliteal swelling first; ± "crescent sign" bruising around the anklerisk factors (immobility, surgery, malignancy)
Investigationultrasound (cyst ± rupture, no clot)Doppler ultrasound (clot), D-dimer
The rule (high-yield): a ruptured Baker's cyst mimics a DVT → always consider and EXCLUDE a DVT (Wells score, D-dimer, Doppler ultrasound) in acute calf swelling — you cannot assume it is a burst cyst. Because the two are clinically indistinguishable, a suspected ruptured cyst is a diagnosis made after excluding DVT.
Note: most ruptures are actually asymptomatic.
Investigations
  • Often a clinical diagnosis (a fluctuant popliteal swelling).
  • Ultrasound — first-line: confirms the cyst (fluid-filled), assesses for rupture, and helps exclude a DVT (no clot).
  • MRI — if diagnostic doubt, or to assess the underlying knee pathology (meniscal tear, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis) in secondary cysts.
  • Exclude DVT if ruptured / acute calf symptoms: Wells score, D-dimer, Doppler ultrasound.
  • In adults, investigate the underlying joint cause (knee X-ray / MRI for osteoarthritis or meniscal tear; assess for rheumatoid arthritis / gout).
Management
Overarching principle: no treatment needed in children; treat the underlying cause in adults; exclude DVT if ruptured.
By group
  • Children → no management needed (primary, benign — resolves spontaneously).
  • Adults → treat the underlying cause — manage the osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, meniscal tear or gout driving it.
Symptomatic / other
  • Analgesia, activity modification.
  • Ultrasound-guided aspiration ± corticosteroid injection for a large / symptomatic cyst.
  • Surgical excision occasionally (recurrent / refractory, with intra-articular pathology addressed).
  • Ruptured cyst → exclude DVT first, then supportive (rest, analgesia, elevation) — usually settles.
The rule (high-yield): treating the underlying knee pathology is the key to managing (and preventing recurrence of) a secondary Baker's cyst.
Exam pearls
What it is
Distension of the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa — a fluid swelling behind the knee (not a true cyst).
Primary vs secondary
Primary = children, benign, no underlying cause. Secondary = adults, marker of knee pathology (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, meniscal tear, gout).
Features
Fluctuant popliteal fossa swelling; often asymptomatic; ± posterior knee tightness / restricted flexion (Foucher's sign).
KEY: rupture mimics DVT
Ruptured cyst → acute calf pain/swelling/redness → always exclude DVT (Wells, D-dimer, Doppler). Most ruptures are asymptomatic.
Investigations
Ultrasound (confirms cyst, excludes DVT); MRI for underlying knee pathology.
Management
Children → none needed. Adults → treat the underlying cause. Aspiration / steroid injection or excision if large/symptomatic.
ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis (Tennis & Go:
Definition & The Core Concept

Epicondylitis = pain + degeneration (a tendinopathy) where the forearm tendons insert onto the elbow epicondyle — a repetitive strain injury.

The core concept: forearm muscles anchor onto the two bony bumps — the medial epicondyle (flexor/pronator origin) and lateral epicondyle (extensor/supinator origin). Overuse inflames/degenerates the common tendon → so which epicondyle hurts tells you which muscle group is overused: medial = wrist flexion, lateral = wrist extension. A clinical diagnosis; self-limiting (though slow). Despite "-itis", more a degenerative tendinopathy.
Symptoms worsen over weeks to months; generally affects middle-aged people.
Lateral (Tennis) vs Medial (Golfer's)
📷 Image placeholder — Elbow anatomy — lateral epicondyle = common extensor/supinator origin (ECRB); medial epicondyle = common flexor/pronator origin with the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel behind it.
🎾 Lateral — tennis elbow
  • Lateral epicondyle; wrist EXTENSORS (esp. extensor carpi radialis brevis)
  • Pain worse on resisted wrist EXTENSION (elbow extended) or resisted supination
  • The commoner of the two
⛳ Medial — golfer's elbow
  • Medial epicondyle; wrist FLEXORS + pronators
  • Pain worse on wrist FLEXION + PRONATION
  • Mnemonic: "golf is a MEDiocre sport" (MEDial)
  • Check for ulnar nerve irritation — it runs behind the medial epicondyle (cubital tunnel)
The rule: lateral = tennis = wrist EXTENSION; medial = golfer's = wrist FLEXION + pronation — the epicondyle and the provoking movement match the overused muscle group.
General Features
  • A repetitive strain injury from overuse of the forearm muscles (sport, occupation, gripping).
  • Symptoms worsen over weeks to months; middle-aged patients.
  • Common to both: pain + tenderness over the affected epicondyle, radiating down the forearm, with weak grip.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Named provocation tests — Cozen's & Mill's (lateral/tennis), Maudsley's / resisted middle-finger extension (lateral); resisted wrist flexion + pronation (medial/golfer's).
A clinical diagnosis — localised epicondyle tenderness + the positive provocation test are usually enough.
Imaging not routinely needed — ultrasound or MRI only if unclear/refractory. Differentials if atypical: cervical radiculopathy, elbow osteoarthritis, ulnar neuritis (medial), radial tunnel syndrome (lateral).
Management
Principle: self-limiting in most — conservative management; it can be slow to resolve.

Rest + activity modification + analgesiaAvoid the provoking movements; simple analgesia / NSAIDs (topical or oral). Reassure — self-limiting (but in some can take years).

What it is
Repetitive-strain tendinopathy at the forearm tendon insertion onto the elbow (degenerative); middle-aged; worsens over weeks–months.
Lateral (TENNIS)
Lateral epicondyle (wrist EXTENSORS) → pain worse on resisted wrist EXTENSION / supination.
Medial (GOLFER's)
Medial epicondyle (wrist FLEXORS + pronators) → pain worse on wrist FLEXION + PRONATION ("golf is a MEDiocre sport").
Both
Epicondyle pain + tenderness, radiates down forearm, weak grip. Medial → check ulnar nerve (cubital tunnel).
Diagnosis
CLINICAL; imaging (ultrasound/MRI) only if unclear or refractory.
Management
Self-limiting → rest + activity modification + analgesia + PHYSIOTHERAPY (eccentric) + counterforce brace; steroid injection/surgery only if refractory.
ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism Syndrome:
Definition & The Core Concept

Fat embolism syndrome (FES) = a systemic condition where fat globules enter the circulation and lodge in small vessels, classically 1–3 days after a long-bone or pelvic fracture (or orthopaedic surgery) → a respiratory + neurological + dermatological syndrome.

The core concept: rib fractures matter for the bone; FES matters for what the marrow releases. When a long bone fractures, fat from the marrow (+ inflammatory mediators) enters the venous circulation → fat emboli travel to the lungs (and, via shunts, brain + skin) → occlude small vessels + trigger a systemic inflammatory response → the classic triad after a latent period of ~24–72 hours.
Largely preventable by early fracture fixation; treatment is supportive. Classically follows long-bone (femur/tibia) + pelvic fractures, especially multiple/closed fractures.

The triad — after a ~24–72h latent periodRespiratory (lungs) + neurological (brain) + petechial rash (skin). The latency distinguishes it from immediate causes.
The Classic Triad
📷 Image placeholder — Non-blanching petechial rash over the axilla/upper trunk and conjunctiva — the most specific (but only ~20–50% prevalent) sign of FES.
🫁 Respiratory — earliest / commonest
  • Tachycardia, dyspnoea, hypoxia → an ARDS-like picture
  • The usual presenting feature
🧠 Neurological

The rash mechanism: embolisation of small dermal capillaries → extravasation of red blood cells — the most specific sign (though only in ~20–50%). Fundoscopy may show retinal haemorrhages + intra-arterial fat globules (Purtscher's-like retinopathy).

Post-fracture respiratory distress has several causes — the timing + the triad distinguish FES.

No specific cure → management is preventive (early fixation) + supportive; steroids have been used as prophylaxis in some settings but are not standard.
Prognosis: most cases are self-limiting and resolve with supportive care (usually within ~1 week); a minority progress to severe respiratory / cerebral failure.

Management
PREVENTION = early long-bone fracture fixation + DVT prophylaxis + supportive care (oxygen/ventilation); no specific cure; usually self-limiting.
ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Band Syndrome:
Definition & The Core Concept

Iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS) = a common overuse / friction injury causing LATERAL KNEE PAIN, especially in runners.

The core concept: the iliotibial band (ITB) runs down the outside of the thigh (tensor fasciae latae / gluteus maximus → Gerdy's tubercle just below the lateral knee). Repeated knee flexion/extension makes it rub against the lateral femoral epicondyle → friction, irritation and pain. A repetitive-strain injury; a clinical diagnosis; conservative management.
The classic exam equation: long-distance runner + lateral knee pain = ITB syndrome.
Lateral Knee Pain — The Differential
CauseDistinguishing features
ITB syndromeLATERAL knee, point tenderness 2–3 cm ABOVE the joint line; overuse (running)
Patellofemoral painanterior / around the patella
Lateral meniscal tearlateral joint LINE, locking/catching, twisting injury
Lateral collateral / biceps femorislateral, but different mechanism
The rule: lateral knee pain + point tenderness 2–3 cm ABOVE the lateral joint line + a runner = ITBS; pain at the joint line (catching / twisting injury) suggests a meniscal tear.
Risk Factors
🏃 Overuse / training
  • Long-distance running, sudden mileage increases
  • Cycling; downhill running
🦵 Biomechanical
  • Weak hip abductors (gluteus medius)
  • Genu varum, excessive foot pronation
  • Cambered surfaces, a tight ITB
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Site of maximal tenderness in ITBS — over the lateral femoral epicondyle, 2–3 cm above the lateral joint line (distinguishing it from joint-line meniscal pain).

Lateral knee painsharp / burning in quality
Tenderness 2–3 cm ABOVE the joint lineover the lateral femoral epicondyle — the characteristic spot
  • Pain worse with running, esp. at ~30° of knee flexion, worse downhill / on stairs; comes on after a predictable distance and eases with rest.
  • No effusion, no locking/catching (distinguishes from intra-articular pathology).
The rule: lateral knee pain (sharp/burning) + tenderness 2–3 cm above the joint line, brought on by running = ITBS.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Noble's and Ober's tests — pressure over the lateral epicondyle while extending the flexed knee reproduces pain (Noble's); Ober's assesses ITB/hip tightness.
A clinical diagnosis — the runner history + characteristic lateral tenderness (± Noble's test: pressure over the lateral epicondyle while extending the flexed knee reproduces pain).
Imaging is not routinely needed — MRI or ultrasound only if the diagnosis is unclear or to exclude other pathology (e.g. a meniscal tear) in refractory cases.
Management
Principle: conservative — activity modification + stretching + hip-abductor strengthening. Most resolve conservatively.

Overuse/friction injury → LATERAL knee pain, classically in RUNNERS.
Mechanism
The ITB rubs against the lateral femoral epicondyle with repeated knee flexion/extension.

ORTHOPAEDICS__Osteochondritis Dissecans:
What & why
Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) = a pathological process affecting SUBCHONDRAL bone (mostly the knee) with secondary effects on the joint cartilage — disruption of the blood supply to an area of bone + cartilage → separation of a fragment of cartilage + underlying bone from the joint surface.
The core concept: OCD is fundamentally a localised osteonecrosis of a segment of subchondral bone — its blood supply fails → the bone (with its overlying cartilage) dies and can separate as an osteochondral fragment. Early on it is vague activity-related knee pain; as the fragment loosens/detaches it becomes a loose body → mechanical symptoms (catching, locking, giving way, a painful clunk). Classically affects children + young adults (often athletic); commonest site = the medial femoral condyle of the knee. Priorities: recognise the mechanical symptoms, use Wilson's sign, image (tunnel-view X-ray + MRI to stage), and treat by whether the fragment is stable or detached.
  • Presents in a young/athletic patient with subacute, post-exercise knee pain ± locking; a cause of a loose body in a young person's knee.
The decisive fork: stable vs unstable/detached
Stable (in situ)Unstable / detached
Fragmentstill attached, viableseparated → a loose body
Symptomsactivity-related paincatching, LOCKING, giving way, painful clunk
Healingcan heal (esp. skeletally immature)won't heal in situ
Managementconservative (rest, restricted activity)surgical (fix or remove ± cartilage repair)
The rule: a stable lesion (especially in a child with open growth plates) can heal with rest; an unstable/detached fragment (mechanical locking, a loose body) needs surgery. Locking/catching/giving way/a clunk = a loose or detached fragment.
Clinical features
📷 Image placeholder — Wilson's sign: knee flexed 90° with the tibia internally rotated, then extended — pain at ~30° relieved by external rotation.
Demographic: children + young adults (often athletic); subacute onset.
FeatureDetail
Knee pain + swellingtypically post-exercise
Mechanical symptomsknee catching / locking / giving way
Painful clunkon flexing/extending the knee → indicates involvement of the LATERAL femoral condyle
Joint effusionon examination
Tendernessover the articular cartilage of the MEDIAL femoral condyle when the knee is flexed (the commonest site)
Wilson's sign (for a medial condyle lesion): knee flexed 90° + tibia INTERNALLY rotated → gradual extension produces PAIN at ~30°, and EXTERNAL rotation of the tibia at this point RELIEVES the pain (internal rotation makes the tibial spine impinge on the classic medial condyle lesion; external rotation moves it away).
The rule: young/athletic patient + post-exercise knee pain + catching/locking + effusion + a positive Wilson's sign = OCD (classically the medial femoral condyle).
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Tunnel (intercondylar/notch) view showing a subchondral crescent lesion of the medial femoral condyle, alongside a T2 MRI demonstrating high-signal fluid behind an unstable fragment.
  • X-ray — AP, lateral, AND TUNNEL view: the tunnel (intercondylar/notch) view best shows the posterior femoral condyle where OCD lesions commonly sit; may show a subchondral crescent sign or loose bodies.
  • MRI — checks the cartilage, visualises loose bodies, and STAGES the lesion (stable vs unstable — is there fluid/signal behind the fragment indicating separation?) → guides management; the most important investigation.
The rule: X-ray (tunnel view — subchondral crescent / loose bodies) → MRI (stage the lesion: stable vs unstable, assess cartilage + loose bodies).
Management
Principle: stable lesions (esp. skeletally immature) → conservative (rest / activity restriction) to allow healing; unstable/detached fragments → surgery (fixation, or removal ± cartilage repair).
Conservative (stable / immature)
  • Activity restriction / relative rest (± restricted weight-bearing/immobilisation), analgesia, physiotherapy → allows healing (better with open growth plates).
Surgical (unstable / detached / loose body)
  • Fixation of a large, viable fragment (pin/screw); drilling of a stable lesion to stimulate healing.
  • Removal of a loose body (arthroscopic) + cartilage restoration (microfracture, osteochondral graft / OATS, autologous chondrocyte implantation) for the defect.
The rule: stable/immature → conservative (rest, let it heal); unstable/detached/loose body → surgery (fix the fragment, or remove it + repair the cartilage). Prognosis is better in skeletally immature patients (open physes → higher healing potential); untreated unstable lesions → loose bodies + early osteoarthritis.
Exam pearls
What it is
Localised loss of blood supply to SUBCHONDRAL bone → a fragment of bone + cartilage can separate (a loose body); children + young adults (athletic); classically the MEDIAL femoral condyle of the knee.
Features
Subacute post-exercise knee pain + swelling; catching/locking/giving way; a painful clunk (lateral condyle); effusion, medial femoral condyle tenderness (flexed).
Wilson's sign
Knee flexed 90° + INTERNAL tibial rotation → extend → pain at ~30°, relieved by EXTERNAL rotation (medial condyle lesion).
Investigations
X-ray (TUNNEL view — subchondral crescent, loose bodies) → MRI (STAGE the lesion — stable vs unstable, cartilage, loose bodies).
Management
Stable/skeletally immature → conservative (rest/activity restriction, heals); unstable/detached/loose body → surgery (fixation, or removal + cartilage repair).
Untreated
Loose bodies + early osteoarthritis.
ORTHOPAEDICS__Rib Fractures & Flail Ches:
Definition & The Core Concept
📷 Image placeholder — Rib fracture level and what lies beneath: 1st/2nd rib = high-energy mechanism (great-vessel/airway injury); lower ribs = liver, spleen, kidney injury.

Rib fracture = a break in the bony segment of any rib, mostly from blunt trauma to the chest wall. Flail chest = a severe complication where a chest-wall segment becomes detached and moves paradoxically.

The core concept: rib fractures matter far less for the broken bone and far MORE for (1) what lies beneath (lung, pleura, vessels) and (2) the effect of PAIN on breathing — pain → splinting (shallow breaths, suppressed cough) → retained secretions → atelectasis + pneumonia. So management is built around adequate analgesia to protect ventilation.
The two don't miss escalations: underlying lung/pleural injury (pneumothorax, haemothorax, contusion) and flail chest. Patterns: 1st/2nd rib = high-energy; lower ribs = liver/spleen/kidney.
Simple vs Complicated — The Escalation Fork

The rule: most = simple → analgesia; but screen for pneumothorax/haemothorax/contusion + flail chest, and note the high-risk patterns (≥3 ribs or elderly = higher morbidity).

ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Neuropathies:
Overview — compression neuropathies
Peripheral nerves compressed as they pass through anatomical tunnels, producing sensory ± motor symptoms in that nerve's distribution.
The organising principle: localise by the nerve and tunnel. Median at the wrist (carpal tunnel); ulnar at the elbow (cubital tunnel); lateral femoral cutaneous at the inguinal ligament (meralgia paraesthetica).
ConditionNerve / siteSymptoms & treatment

Look for reversible/associated causes of carpal tunnel — pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, acromegaly, rheumatoid arthritis. Thenar wasting or constant numbness → urgent decompression.
What & why
Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) = compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist (deep to the flexor retinaculum / transverse carpal ligament) — the commonest entrapment neuropathy.
The core concept: the carpal tunnel is a rigid, unyielding space (carpal bones + flexor retinaculum) through which the median nerve + flexor tendons pass. Anything that reduces the space or swells its contents compresses the median nerve → a very predictable picture: sensory symptoms in the median territory (lateral 3½ fingers), worse at night, relieved by shaking the hand, and eventually thenar wasting. Priorities: recognise the classic median pattern (and its causes), and manage stepwise (splint → injection → decompression).
  • Commoner in women, often bilateral; frequently idiopathic but with important secondary associations.
The decisive fork: is this CTS or a mimic?

The palmar-sparing clue: the palmar cutaneous branch arises BEFORE the carpal tunnel → sensation over the THENAR EMINENCE skin is SPARED in CTS → distinguishes it from a more proximal median lesion.
The rule: CTS = median sensory symptoms (lateral 3½ fingers), sparing the thenar eminence skin, worse at night.
Median nerve & carpal tunnel anatomy
📷 Image placeholder — Carpal-tunnel cross-section — median nerve and flexor tendons beneath the flexor retinaculum, with the median (lateral 3½-finger) sensory territory shaded
  • Tunnel contents: the median nerve + the flexor tendons (FDS, FDP, FPL), roofed by the flexor retinaculum.
  • Motor — the LOAF muscles: Lumbricals (lateral 2), Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis → the thenar muscles (thumb abduction/opposition); these waste in advanced CTS.
  • Sensory: the lateral (radial) 3½ fingers — thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger (palmar).
Causes
CategoryCauses

The rule: new CTS → check for pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly (treatable secondary causes).
Clinical features
  • Sensory (early): pain, tingling, numbness, paraesthesia in the median distribution (lateral 3½ fingers); classically WORSE AT NIGHT (wakes the patient), relieved by shaking/dangling the hand ("flick sign") — the hallmark.
  • Motor (late): weakness of thumb abduction/opposition + THENAR WASTING (LOAF muscles) → clumsiness, dropping things.
  • Provocation signs: Tinel's (percussing over the median nerve reproduces tingling); Phalen's (forced wrist flexion ~60 s reproduces symptoms).
The rule: median sensory symptoms worse at night, relieved by shaking the hand, ± thenar wasting, with positive Tinel's/Phalen's = CTS.
Investigations
  • Largely a clinical diagnosis (characteristic history + Tinel's/Phalen's).
  • Nerve conduction studies (NCS) — confirmatory: slowed median conduction across the wrist (prolonged distal latency); confirm diagnosis + severity and exclude other lesions.
  • Investigate secondary causes: TFTs, glucose/HbA1c, pregnancy test; ultrasound can show median nerve swelling.
The rule: clinical diagnosis; NCS confirms + grades severity.
Management (stepwise)
Principle: conservative → injection → surgery; and treat any underlying cause (pregnancy-related CTS often resolves after delivery — temporise with a splint).
  • 1st — conservative: wrist splint (especially at night) holding the wrist neutral; activity modification.
  • 2nd — corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel — reduces swelling; effective, often temporising.
  • 3rd — surgery: carpal tunnel decompression (division of the flexor retinaculum) — for severe/persistent symptoms, motor involvement or failed conservative treatment.
Escalation rule: splint → steroid injection → surgical decompression; operate early if thenar wasting / motor signs (to prevent permanent weakness).

What it is
Median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel (under the flexor retinaculum); commonest entrapment neuropathy; women, often bilateral.
Sensory

Motor (late)

Causes
Idiopathic; pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, obesity, repetitive use.
Ix + management
Clinical; NCS confirm. Treat cause + wrist splint (night) → steroid injection → decompression; operate early if thenar wasting.
What & why
Cubital tunnel syndrome = compression of the ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel at the elbow, behind the medial epicondyle (the "funny bone") — the second commonest entrapment neuropathy.
The core concept: the ulnar nerve runs superficially behind the medial epicondyle through the tight cubital tunnel, vulnerable to compression, stretch or repeated trauma — especially with the elbow flexed (which tightens the tunnel). This gives a predictable ulnar picture: tingling/numbness of the little + ring fingers, worse with elbow flexion, and eventually intrinsic wasting → claw hand. The elbow is to the ulnar nerve what the wrist is to the median.
The decisive fork: cubital vs carpal vs other
Cubital tunnel (ulnar @ elbow)Carpal tunnel (median @ wrist)
Sensorymedial 1½ fingers (little + ½ ring)lateral 3½ fingers
Motorintrinsic hand muscles (all except LOAF) → claw handthenar (LOAF) → thenar wasting

The rule: cubital tunnel = ulnar nerve, at the elbow → medial 1½ fingers + intrinsic wasting/claw hand, worse on elbow flexion.
Other differentials: C8/T1 radiculopathy (dermatomal, neck pain), thoracic outlet syndrome (whole limb), ulnar compression at Guyon's canal (wrist-level ulnar lesion).
The ulnar nerve
📷 Image placeholder — Ulnar claw hand (hyperextended MCP + flexed IP of the 4th/5th fingers) with the medial 1½-finger sensory territory
  • Motor: supplies ALL intrinsic hand muscles EXCEPT the LOAF muscles — i.e. interossei, medial 2 lumbricals, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis → finger abduction/adduction + grip.
  • Sensory: the medial 1½ fingers (little + medial half of ring), palmar + dorsal.
  • Course: passes behind the medial epicondyle (superficial, vulnerable) → through the cubital tunnel → forearm/hand.
Causes
  • Compression / stretch at the cubital tunnel: prolonged elbow flexion (sleeping bent, phone use), leaning on the elbow (desk work), repetitive elbow movements.
  • Direct trauma/pressure to the medial elbow; elbow osteoarthritis, medial epicondyle fracture, or cubitus valgus (a "tardy ulnar palsy" years after an old elbow injury).
The rule: anything that compresses or stretches the ulnar nerve at the elbow — especially sustained elbow flexion + leaning on the elbow.
Clinical features
  • Sensory (early): tingling + numbness of the 4th + 5th fingers (medial 1½), worse on elbow flexion (often wakes the patient with a bent elbow).
  • Motor (later): weakness + wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles → weak grip, weak finger abduction/adduction; ulnar claw hand (hyperextended MCP + flexed IP of the 4th/5th fingers).
  • Froment's sign: weak adductor pollicis → the patient flexes the thumb IP joint (using median FPL) to grip paper — a sign of ulnar motor weakness.
The ulnar paradox: a more PROXIMAL (elbow) lesion produces a LESS obvious claw than a distal (wrist) lesion — because the proximal lesion also paralyses the ulnar FDP to the ring/little fingers (so they flex less, making the claw less pronounced).
The rule: ulnar tingling (little + ring) worse on elbow flexion, ± intrinsic wasting/claw = cubital tunnel syndrome.
Investigations
  • Largely a clinical diagnosis (ulnar distribution + elbow-level provocation).
  • Nerve conduction studies (NCS): slowed ulnar conduction across the elbow — localises the lesion to the cubital tunnel + grades severity; distinguishes from a wrist (Guyon's) or root lesion.
  • Elbow exam: Tinel's over the cubital tunnel, elbow-flexion test; assess for wasting/claw/Froment's.
The rule: clinical diagnosis; NCS confirms + localises to the elbow.
Management
Principle: conservative first (avoid elbow flexion/pressure + splinting); surgical decompression/transposition for severe or refractory disease.
  • 1st — conservative: avoid provoking positions (don't lean on the elbow, avoid sustained flexion); elbow splinting in extension, especially at night; elbow padding.
  • 2nd — surgery: decompression of the cubital tunnel ± ulnar nerve transposition (moving the nerve anterior to the medial epicondyle) — for severe/progressive/refractory disease or motor involvement.
Escalation rule: avoid elbow flexion/pressure + night splint → surgical decompression/transposition; operate early if intrinsic wasting.

What & why
Meralgia paraesthetica = paraesthesia or anaesthesia in the distribution of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN), caused by compression/entrapment of the LFCN.
The core concept: the LFCN is a PURELY SENSORY nerve (L2/3) supplying the skin over the lateral thigh, subject to repeated pressure/compression as it passes under the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS). Because it is sensory only, the whole picture is sensory disturbance over the lateral thigh with NO motor weakness — this pure-sensory, well-localised pattern is the diagnostic key. It is usually benign + self-limiting; remove the compressive cause (often weight/tight clothing) and confirm with a nerve block if needed.

Clinical features
  • Symptoms over the UPPER LATERAL thigh: burning, tingling, coldness or shooting pain; numbness; deep muscle ache.
  • Positional pattern: worse on STANDING, better on SITTING (standing/hip extension stretches the nerve; sitting/hip flexion relaxes it).
  • On examination: NO motor weakness (the key sign — pure sensory nerve); altered sensation over the lateral thigh; symptoms reproduced by deep palpation below the ASIS + hip extension.
The rule: well-localised lateral-thigh sensory disturbance, worse on standing, NO motor weakness, reproduced by palpation below the ASIS = meralgia paraesthetica.
Investigations
  • Largely a clinical diagnosis (the characteristic sensory pattern).
  • Pelvic compression test — very sensitive; often diagnoses it alone (compressing the pelvis relaxes the inguinal ligament and relieves symptoms).
  • Diagnostic nerve block — local anaesthetic injection abolishes the pain: confirms the diagnosis and can be therapeutic.
  • Ultrasound — good for diagnosis + guiding injection therapy. If atypical, consider NCS / imaging to exclude a lumbar/pelvic lesion compressing L2/3.
The rule: clinical diagnosis; the pelvic compression test is very sensitive, and a local anaesthetic nerve block confirms it.
Management
Principle: conservative — remove the compressive cause; usually self-limiting; escalate to injection/surgery if refractory.
  • Conservative (first-line, the mainstay): weight loss, loose clothing (avoid tight belts), activity modification; reassurance (usually benign + self-limiting; pregnancy-related resolves after delivery); analgesia ± neuropathic agents (amitriptyline, gabapentin/pregabalin).
  • 2nd — local anaesthetic ± corticosteroid injection (nerve block — diagnostic + therapeutic; can be ultrasound-guided).
  • 3rd — surgery (rarely needed): nerve decompression or (rarely) transection for severe, persistent, refractory cases.
The rule: conservative (weight loss, loose clothing, analgesia) → nerve block → surgery if refractory.

Overview — hand & wrist disorders

What & why
De Quervain's tenosynovitis = swelling + inflammation of the tendon sheaths at the wrist — specifically abductor pollicis longus (AbPL) + extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) — a repetitive strain injury causing pain on the RADIAL side of the wrist.
The core concept: two thumb tendons (AbPL + EPB) run together through the first extensor (dorsal) compartment at the radial wrist, beneath the extensor retinaculum. Repetitive thumb/wrist movement inflames + swells their shared sheath → the tendons no longer glide smoothly through the tight tunnel → radial-sided wrist pain. So it reduces to: radial wrist pain near the base of the thumb, worse with thumb/wrist movement. The clinical hallmark is a single positive test — Finkelstein's — and management is conservative.
  • Classically affects people with repetitive thumb use — new mothers (lifting babies), texting/typing, occupational tasks ("mother's/gamer's thumb").
The decisive fork: radial wrist / thumb pain

Dupuytren's contracture = the fascia of the hand becomes thickened + tight → finger contractures — a progressive fibrosis (fibromatosis) of the palmar fascia.
The core concept: the palmar fascia thickens, develops nodules, and forms cords that extend into the fingers and pull them into flexion — so the finger cannot fully extend (a contracture). The picture: a painless, slowly progressive flexion contracture, usually of the ring finger, in a patient with typical risk factors (family history, alcohol, diabetes). It is a clinical diagnosis (palpable cord/nodule + the table-top test); the key decision is when to operate — once the fingers can't be straightened / laid flat.
  • Usually NO pain — it is loss of extension, not pain, that brings patients in; mostly the ring finger.

What & why
Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis) = pain + difficulty moving a finger from a disparity between the size of the tendon and the pulleys it passes through — the tendon becomes stuck and can't pass smoothly through the pulley.
The core concept: the flexor tendons run through pulleys holding them against bone. If the tendon (or sheath) thickens — often forming a nodule — it no longer glides through the tight first (A1) pulley at the MCP joint → the finger catches, then locks in flexion, then releases suddenly with a painful pop/click. So it is a mechanical size-mismatch: a swollen tendon squeezing through an unyielding pulley. Signature: a finger that catches/locks in a bent position and snaps straight, worst in the morning. Clinical diagnosis; steroid injection is highly effective.
  • Idiopathic in most; risk factors: women, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes.

  • Thickening/tightening of the tendon sheath → the tendon can't move smoothly when the finger flexes + extends → stiffness or catching.
  • Most commonly affects the first annular (A1) pulley at the MCP joint; there may be a NODULE on the tendon.
  • When FLEXED, the nodule sits proximal to the A1 pulley; as the finger EXTENDS, the nodule gets STUCK at the entrance to the A1 pulley → the finger LOCKS in flexion, then releases suddenly with a painful POP/CLICK (the "trigger").
The rule: tendon nodule + tight A1 pulley → the nodule can't slide back through on extension → finger locks in flexion → releases with a snap.
Risk factors & clinical features
  • Idiopathic in most; associations: women, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes mellitus (the "diabetic hand").

The rule: catching/locking of the thumb/middle/ring finger, worse in the morning, with palm-side MCP tenderness + a palpable nodule = trigger finger.

A clinical diagnosis (the trigger + nodule) — no imaging needed.

1st line: steroid injectioninto the tendon sheath at the A1 pulley — successful in most patients

The rule: steroid injection (1st-line, works in most) → splint → surgical A1 pulley release if refractory.

Stenosing tenosynovitis — size mismatch between the flexor tendon (± a nodule) and the A1 pulley at the MCP → the tendon catches.

Finger CATCHES/LOCKS in flexion → releases with a painful POP/CLICK ("trigger"); a nodule at the MCP (palm-side); worse in the morning.

Thumb, middle, ring most common.

Idiopathic (most); women, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis.

Trigger finger = painful, catches/snaps; Dupuytren's = painless, fixed flexion, no snapping (fascial cord).

Corticosteroid injection (1st-line, effective in most) → splint → surgical A1 pulley release if refractory.
What & why
Ganglion cyst = a benign cyst arising from a joint or tendon sheath — a fluid-filled swelling most often around the dorsal aspect of the wrist.
The core concept: a benign, fluid-filled (synovial) cyst that balloons out from a joint capsule or tendon sheath via a stalk, filled with thick, jelly-like synovial fluid. This explains its two useful features: it is firm, well-circumscribed, and TRANSILLUMINATES (light passes through the clear fluid — distinguishing it from a solid tumour), and it is completely benign. The message: recognise it, reassure, and usually leave it alone — most need no treatment and many resolve spontaneously. Intervene only for significant symptoms or neurovascular compromise. It is the commonest soft-tissue lump of the hand + wrist.
  • Common; often on the dorsal wrist; painless in most (sometimes an ache or cosmetic concern).

The rule: a firm, transilluminating, well-circumscribed swelling on the dorsal wrist, often painless = ganglion.

  • A clinical diagnosis — site + a firm, transilluminating, well-circumscribed swelling is usually sufficient.
  • Transillumination (shine a light through it) confirms it is cystic, not solid.
  • Ultrasound if uncertain (confirms a cyst; assesses the connection / any solid component); MRI rarely, for atypical/deep lesions or to exclude a solid tumour.
The rule: clinical diagnosis (+ transillumination); imaging only if atypical.
Management
Principle: reassurance — most resolve spontaneously; intervene only for severe symptoms or neurovascular problems.

The rule: reassure + observe (most resolve); aspiration or surgical excision only for troublesome symptoms/neurovascular compromise (both can recur). Do NOT hit it with a heavy book ("Bible therapy" — ineffective and harmful).

ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disorders:
Overview — shoulder disorders
Common causes of shoulder pain and restricted movement arising from the rotator cuff, the joint capsule and the biceps tendon.
The organising principle: the pattern of restriction localises it. Active > passive limitation → rotator cuff; loss of both active and passive movement (especially external rotation) → frozen shoulder; sudden pop + “Popeye” bulge → biceps rupture.
ConditionKey signManagement
Rotator cuff disorderspainful arc; weak abduction/external rotationphysiotherapy, injection; repair if full-thickness tear
Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis)global stiffness, external rotation most lost; diabetesself-limiting (1–3 years); physio ± injection
Biceps tendon rupturesudden pop, “Popeye” deformityusually conservative
Frozen shoulder is strongly associated with diabetes — check glucose. Loss of passive range points to the capsule, not the cuff.
What & why
Rotator cuff disorders = a spectrum affecting the rotator cuff muscles/tendons — from impingement/tendinopathy to partial or full-thickness TEARS — from an acute injury, degenerative ageing, or overhead activities (e.g. tennis).
The core concept: the rotator cuff (the SITS muscles) dynamically stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid + produces fine shoulder movements. Because these tendons pass through a tight subacromial space, they are prone to impingement, degeneration and tearing — and since each muscle has a specific action, the pattern of weakness localises which tendon is torn. The approach: know the SITS anatomy + actions → the positive special test tells you the tendon; and the management fork is degenerative (conservative) vs acute/full-thickness in a young/active patient (surgery). Hallmarks: shoulder pain, weakness on specific movements, difficulty sleeping.
  • Very common (age + overhead activity); supraspinatus is the most commonly affected tendon.
The decisive fork: degenerative vs acute
DegenerativeAcute / young-active / full-thickness
Causeage-related degenerationacute injury; overhead athlete
Tearoften partial, attritionalfull-thickness / traumatic
Patientolder, lower demandyoung, active, high-demand
Managementconservativesurgery (arthroscopic repair)
The rule: degenerative cuff tears → conservative (rest, activity modification, analgesia, physiotherapy); acute tears / young-active patients / full-thickness tears → surgery (arthroscopic rotator cuff repair).
Anatomy: the SITS muscles

The rule: SITS — Supraspinatus (abduction, first 15°), Infraspinatus + Teres minor (external rotation), Subscapularis (internal rotation) → the action tells you the tendon; a positive test on a given movement localises the tear. Supraspinatus is the most commonly torn (passes under the acromion → most prone to impingement); tested by the "empty can" test.
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Onseteither acute (after an injury) OR gradual
Shoulder pain± referred to the deltoid region

Difficulty sleepingcan't get comfortable; classically can't lie on the affected shoulder
Localising: weak abduction → supraspinatus; weak external rotation → infraspinatus/teres minor; weak internal rotation → subscapularis. A painful arc (~60–120° of abduction) suggests subacromial impingement / supraspinatus.
The rule: shoulder pain + WEAKNESS on specific movements (localises the tendon) + difficulty sleeping (night pain) = rotator cuff disease.
Investigations
TestAssesses
"Empty can" (Jobe's) testsupraspinatus (resisted abduction in the empty-can position)

  • MRI — best for full-thickness tears, tear size/retraction, surgical planning.
  • X-ray — excludes other causes (osteoarthritis, calcific tendinitis, acromial shape); a high-riding humeral head suggests a large chronic tear.
The rule: clinical (special tests localise the tendon) → ultrasound/MRI to confirm + size the tear.
Management
Principle: degenerative → conservative; young/active or full-thickness → surgical repair.
  • Degenerative — conservative: rest + adapted activities (avoid aggravating overhead movements), analgesia (NSAIDs), and physiotherapy (the cornerstone — strengthen the cuff + scapular stabilisers, restore range); ± subacromial corticosteroid injection for pain/impingement.
  • Active/young patients OR full-thickness tears — surgery: arthroscopic rotator cuff repair — the tendon is reattached to bone (keyhole surgery).
The rule: conservative first for degenerative disease (physiotherapy is key); arthroscopic repair for acute full-thickness tears / young active / high-demand patients.

What it is
Spectrum from impingement/tendinopathy → partial/full-thickness TEARS; from acute injury, age-related degeneration, or overhead activity.
SITS (+ actions)
Supraspinatus (abduction, first 15°) · Infraspinatus + Teres minor (external rotation) · Subscapularis (internal rotation + adduction); supraspinatus most commonly torn.
Features
Shoulder pain + WEAKNESS on specific movements (localises the tendon) + difficulty sleeping; painful arc (60–120°) = impingement/supraspinatus.
Tests
Empty can (supraspinatus), resisted external rotation (infraspinatus/teres minor), lift-off (subscapularis); ultrasound/MRI confirm + size the tear.
Management
Degenerative → conservative (rest, analgesia, PHYSIOTHERAPY ± steroid injection); acute / young-active / full-thickness → arthroscopic rotator cuff repair.
Most torn
Supraspinatus (under the acromion → most impinged).
What & why
Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) = a common cause of shoulder pain + stiffness, from inflammation + fibrosis of the glenohumeral joint CAPSULE → adhesions that tighten the capsule + restrict movement — mostly affecting middle-aged females.
The core concept: the problem is the joint CAPSULE itself — inflamed, then fibrosed, forming adhesions (scar tissue) that bind + contract the capsule. This gives the defining sign that separates it from every other shoulder problem: BOTH active AND passive movement are restricted — the capsule is physically tight, so the shoulder won't move even when the examiner moves it (unlike a cuff tear, where passive range is preserved). It has a self-limiting but PROLONGED three-phase course (painful → stiff → thawing) over 1–3 years, and the strongest risk factor is diabetes. Management is largely symptomatic + patience — no single intervention clearly changes the outcome.
  • External rotation is the most affected movement; a clinical diagnosis of exclusion.
The decisive fork: frozen shoulder vs cuff tear vs osteoarthritis
Frozen shoulderRotator cuff tearGlenohumeral OA
Passive movementRESTRICTED (active + passive)preserved (only active limited)restricted
Problemcapsular fibrosis / adhesionstendon tear (weakness)joint degeneration
Most affectedexternal rotationmovement of the torn tendonglobal
X-raynormalnormal (± high-riding head)OA changes
The rule: frozen shoulder = BOTH active AND passive movement restricted (a tight capsule), external rotation most affected, X-ray NORMAL. The restriction of PASSIVE movement is the key — even the examiner can't move the shoulder → distinguishes it from a cuff tear (passive range preserved) and osteoarthritis (X-ray changes).
Pathophysiology & risk factors
  • Pathophysiology: the glenohumeral joint capsule undergoes inflammation → fibrosis → adhesions that bind + tighten the capsule → restricted movement.
  • Risk factors: the key one is DIABETES MELLITUS (strongly associated, often more severe/bilateral); middle-aged females; also thyroid disease, prolonged immobilisation, previous shoulder injury/surgery, Dupuytren's.
The rule: capsular inflammation → fibrosis → adhesions → a tight, contracted capsule; think DIABETES.
Clinical features & the three phases

Key examination findings: external rotation most affected; stiffness affects BOTH active AND passive movement (the defining sign).
PhaseDetail
1. Painful phasepain-predominant (often the presenting phase; worse at night)
2. Stiff (frozen) phasestiffness-predominant, pain settles

The course: painful → stiff → thawing, over 1–3 years; up to 50% have persistent symptoms — self-limiting but slow, and not always complete.
Investigations
  • A clinical diagnosis based on history + examination (global restriction of active + passive movement, especially external rotation).
  • X-ray to exclude osteoarthritis — should be NORMAL in frozen shoulder.
  • Ultrasound, CT or MRI will show a THICKENED joint capsule (supports the diagnosis if needed).
The rule: clinical diagnosis; X-ray normal (excludes osteoarthritis); ultrasound/MRI shows a thickened capsule.
Management
Principle: no single intervention clearly improves the outcome — symptomatic management (analgesia, physiotherapy, steroids) while it runs its course; surgery (manipulation under anaesthesia / capsular release) for refractory cases.
  • NSAIDs — analgesia, esp. in the painful phase.
  • Physiotherapy — maintain/restore range (gentle stretching).
  • Oral / intra-articular corticosteroids — reduce inflammation/pain, esp. early.
  • Surgery: manipulation under anaesthesia (MUA) — forcefully stretch the capsule to break the adhesions; ± arthroscopic capsular release.
  • Optimise diabetes (the key risk factor).
The rule: because no single treatment clearly changes the natural history, management is symptomatic + supportive through the phases (analgesia + steroids early for pain, physiotherapy to preserve range), reserving MUA/capsular release for refractory cases.

Inflammation + fibrosis of the joint CAPSULE → adhesions → a tight, restricted capsule; middle-aged women; key risk factor = DIABETES.

Painful → stiff (frozen) → thawing; lasts 1–3 years (self-limiting but slow; up to 50% have persistent symptoms).

Clinical diagnosis; X-ray NORMAL (excludes osteoarthritis); ultrasound/MRI → thickened capsule.
Management
No single intervention clearly helps → symptomatic: NSAIDs + physiotherapy + oral/intra-articular corticosteroids; manipulation under anaesthesia / capsular release for refractory cases.

Diabetes (the key risk factor).
What & why
Biceps tendon rupture = one of the biceps tendons separates from its attachment or tears across its full width. The biceps has two proximal tendons (long + short head) at the origin and one distal tendon onto the radial tuberosity.
The core concept: which tendon ruptures determines everything — the mechanism, where the "pop" is felt, the deformity, and whether it needs surgery. The proximal LONG HEAD is by far the commonest; because the short head + brachialis compensate, it is largely a cosmetic (Popeye deformity) problem managed CONSERVATIVELY. A DISTAL rupture causes meaningful functional loss (esp. supination/flexion power) and needs SURGICAL repair. So one rule organises it: proximal (long head) → conservative; distal → surgery. The tendon is often already degenerate (age, overuse, steroids, smoking), so ruptures occur with modest force.
  • Presents with a sudden "pop" + pain after a load on a contracting biceps; the Popeye deformity is the classic sign of a proximal rupture.

The rule: sudden pop + pain/bruising/swelling + Popeye deformity + weakness (esp. supination) = biceps tendon rupture.
Investigations
  • Biceps squeeze test: squeeze the biceps muscle belly — an intact tendon → forearm SUPINATION; no supination → a ruptured (distal) tendon (analogous to the Simmonds/Thompson's calf-squeeze test for the Achilles).
  • MSK ultrasound — first-line: confirms the rupture + location.
  • Urgent MRI for a suspected distal rupture — best defines a distal tear (which needs prompt surgery — retraction worsens with time).

Management
Principle: proximal (long head) → conservative; distal → surgical (and promptly).

DistalSURGICAL — repair/reattach the tendon to the radial tuberosity
The rule: distal ruptures should be repaired PROMPTLY (within ~2–3 weeks) — the tendon retracts + scars, making late repair harder and recovery poorer. Proximal/long head → conservative (cosmetic, function preserved); distal → surgical repair (restores supination/flexion power).

Proximal → conservative; distal → surgery.
ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle Disorders:
Overview — foot & ankle disorders
Common foot and ankle soft-tissue problems affecting the Achilles tendon, the lateral ligament complex and the plantar fascia.
The organising principle: mechanism + site of tenderness. Achilles (tendinopathy vs rupture — the calf-squeeze test); lateral ligament sprain (inversion injury — Ottawa rules for X-ray); plantar fascia (inferior heel pain worst on the first steps).
ConditionClueManagement
Achilles tendon disordersposterior heel; rupture → sudden “kick”, positive Simmonds' testtendinopathy: load/physio; rupture: immobilise in equinus ± surgery
Ankle sprains & ligament injuriesinversion injury → ATFL; use Ottawa ankle rulesRICE, early mobilisation, rehab
Plantar fasciitisinferior heel pain worst on first stepsstretching, orthotics; self-limiting
Don't miss Achilles rupture — a palpable gap and positive Simmonds' (calf-squeeze) test, even if the patient can still weakly plantarflex. Use the Ottawa rules to avoid unnecessary ankle X-rays.
What & why
Achilles tendon disorders = a spectrum from tendinopathy (overuse degeneration) to complete rupture of the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon — the commonest cause of posterior heel pain.
The core concept: the Achilles is the tendon of gastrocnemius + soleus onto the calcaneus — it plantarflexes the foot. Two things go wrong at opposite ends of a spectrum: chronic overuse → tendinopathy (gradual heel pain) and sudden overload → rupture (acute "pop"). The key task is not to miss a rupture — because a ruptured Achilles can still appear to plantarflex (other muscles compensate), so diagnosis rests on the calf-squeeze (Simmonds'/Thompson's) test. Both share the same risk factors: fluoroquinolones and hypercholesterolaemia.
  • Ultrasound is the key first-line imaging for a suspected rupture.

The rule: gradual heel pain worse after activity + preserved calf-squeeze = tendinopathy; sudden "pop" + palpable gap + LOST calf-squeeze plantarflexion = rupture. The calf-squeeze test separates them.
Shared risk factors: quinolones (ciprofloxacin) and hypercholesterolaemia predispose to both.

  • Quinolone antibiotics (e.g. ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) — a classic cause of Achilles tendinopathy and rupture (an MHRA warning; stop the quinolone if tendon pain develops).
  • Hypercholesterolaemia (lipid deposition in the tendon / xanthomata).
  • Also: increasing age, a sudden increase in training / unaccustomed activity, corticosteroids (systemic or local injection), diabetes, gout, inflammatory arthritis, obesity, poor footwear.

  • Examination: squeezing the calf → plantarflexion of the foot (calf-squeeze NORMAL — the tendon is intact).
  • Management: supportive — analgesia + eccentric calf-strengthening exercises (the key active treatment); activity modification, heel raises/orthotics; avoid corticosteroid injection (increases rupture risk).
The rule: gradual heel pain, worse after activity, morning stiffness, intact calf-squeeze = tendinopathy → supportive management + eccentric calf exercises.
Achilles tendon rupture

Suspect if the patient heard a "pop" while playing sport, with sudden significant pain — often "kicked/hit in the back of the leg".

Investigation + management: 1st line = ultrasound (confirms rupture + gap) → acute orthopaedic referral. Conservative = immobilise in a boot/plaster in plantarflexion (equinus) then graduated rehab; surgical repair for selected patients (younger/athletes, delayed presentation, re-rupture). Keep immobilised in equinus / non-weight-bearing until seen.

Commonest cause of posterior heel pain; spectrum tendinopathy → rupture.

What & why
An ankle sprain = a stretching, partial, or complete tear of a ligament around the ankle — one of the commonest musculoskeletal injuries.
The core concept: ankle sprains split into two very different injuries by which ligament complex is torn: "low" sprains (LATERAL collateral ligaments — inversion — >90%, common + benign) and "high" sprains (the SYNDESMOSIS — external rotation — rarer, more serious, slower to heal). Priorities: distinguish low from high, use the Ottawa ankle rules to decide on an X-ray (exclude fracture), and — for high sprains — check for diastasis (tibiofibular separation), which changes management to surgery. Most low sprains are conservative (RICE).
  • Contrast with an ankle fracture (Weber classification) — the Ottawa rules triage between them.

Low ankle sprain (lateral ligament)

The rule: external rotation + very painful weight-bearing + positive squeeze test = high (syndesmotic) ankle sprain.
Investigations
Ottawa ankle rules — decide whether an X-ray is needed: X-ray only if pain in the malleolar zone AND one of: inability to weight-bear for 4 steps; bony tenderness over the distal tibia (posterior edge/tip of the medial malleolus); or bony tenderness over the distal fibula (posterior edge/tip of the lateral malleolus). Purpose: minimise unnecessary X-rays (highly sensitive for clinically significant fractures).
  • Low sprain: X-ray if persistent pain (± check peroneal tendons).
  • High sprain: radiographs show WIDENING of the tibiofibular joint (diastasis); MRI if high suspicion of syndesmotic injury but the X-ray is normal.
The rule: use the Ottawa rules to decide on X-ray; high sprain → look for tibiofibular widening (diastasis); MRI if X-ray normal but suspicion is high.
Management
Principle: low sprains → conservative (RICE); high sprains → conservative if stable/no diastasis, surgery if diastasis or failed non-operative treatment.
Low ankle sprain
  • RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation).
  • Short-term relief with a removable orthosis, cast, or crutches.
  • Early mobilisation + physiotherapy / rehab (proprioception, strengthening) to prevent chronic instability.
High ankle sprain
  • No diastasis → non-weight-bearing orthosis or cast until pain subsides.
  • Diastasis, or failed non-operative management → operative fixation.
  • Diastasis = separation of the tibia and fibula (the key decision point).
Contrast — ankle fractures: managed by the Weber classification (A below / B at / C above the syndesmosis) — CAM boot for stable, ORIF for unstable/syndesmotic.

Stretch/tear of an ankle ligament; LOW (lateral collateral — ATFL/CFL/PTFL) vs HIGH (syndesmosis).
Low (>90%)
INVERSION, ATFL most common, lateral tenderness (anterior/inferior to the lateral malleolus), usually can weight-bear → RICE + brace/rehab; graded I–III.
High (syndesmotic)
EXTERNAL ROTATION, syndesmosis (AITFL/PITFL/interosseous), very painful weight-bearing, positive HOPKINS SQUEEZE TEST → check for diastasis.

X-ray if malleolar-zone pain + [can't weight-bear 4 steps, OR bony tenderness at distal tibia OR distal fibula].
High-sprain imaging
X-ray shows tibiofibular WIDENING (diastasis); MRI if X-ray normal but suspicion high.
Management
Low → RICE/brace; high → cast if no diastasis, SURGERY if diastasis or failed conservative. Contrast ankle fractures → Weber A/B/C.
What & why
Plantar fasciitis = a degenerative/inflammatory condition of the plantar fascia (the fibrous band from the calcaneus to the toes, supporting the arch) — the commonest cause of heel pain in adults.
The core concept: the plantar fascia supports the arch and takes tensile load with every step; overuse/repetitive microtrauma at its origin (the medial calcaneal tuberosity) → degeneration + pain (despite "-itis", largely degenerative). This gives a near-diagnostic pattern: inferior heel pain worst on the first steps in the morning (or after rest), easing with activity. Priorities: recognise the pattern, localise tenderness to the medial calcaneal tuberosity, and exclude the mimics. It is a clinical diagnosis and self-limiting.
  • Associated with prolonged standing, running, obesity, poor footwear, and a tight Achilles/calf.

Clinical features
  • Heel pain worse around the MEDIAL CALCANEAL TUBEROSITY (the plantar fascia origin — inferior + slightly medial heel), unlike Achilles tendinopathy (worse higher, at the tendon insertion).
  • Classic pattern: pain worst on the FIRST STEPS in the morning (or after rest), then eases with activity (may worsen again after prolonged standing / end of day) — the hallmark "first-step pain".
  • Tenderness on palpation of the medial calcaneal tuberosity; pain worse on dorsiflexion of the toes (the windlass mechanism tensions the fascia).
The rule: inferior heel pain, worst on the first steps in the morning, tender over the medial calcaneal tuberosity = plantar fasciitis.
Risk factors
  • Mechanical/overuse: prolonged standing (occupational), running/jumping sports, a sudden increase in activity, obesity, poor/unsupportive footwear, flat feet (pes planus) or high arches, a tight Achilles/calf.
  • Bilateral heel pain / a young patient → consider a seronegative spondyloarthropathy (enthesitis).
Investigations
  • A clinical diagnosis (characteristic history + tenderness over the medial calcaneal tuberosity) — no investigations usually needed.
  • Imaging only if atypical/refractory: X-ray may show a calcaneal (heel) spur (common, often incidental — NOT the cause) or exclude a stress fracture; ultrasound/MRI can show fascia thickening.
  • Thompson's/Simmonds' test to exclude an Achilles rupture if that is a consideration.
The rule: clinical diagnosis; imaging reserved for doubt/refractory cases (a heel spur on X-ray is often incidental).
Management
Principle: conservative — rest, supportive footwear, insoles/heel pads, and stretching; self-limiting (though often slow).
  • Rest the feet where possible (activity modification — reduce standing/impact).
  • Supportive footwear — good arch support + cushioned heels; insoles + heel pads to offload the fascia origin.
  • Plantar fascia + calf/Achilles stretching — the key active treatment; analgesia / NSAIDs, ice, weight loss; night splints (hold the ankle dorsiflexed overnight).
  • If refractory: corticosteroid injection (short-term relief; small risk of fascia rupture / fat-pad atrophy → judicious), extracorporeal shockwave therapy; rarely surgery (plantar fascia release).
Reassurance: plantar fasciitis is self-limiting — the majority resolve within ~6–12 months with conservative measures.
Exam pearls

Commonest cause of adult heel pain; degenerative overuse of the plantar fascia origin.
Features
Inferior heel pain at the MEDIAL CALCANEAL TUBEROSITY, worst on the FIRST STEPS in the morning / after rest, eases with activity; worse on toe dorsiflexion.
Differentials
Achilles tendinopathy (higher/posterior — Thompson's excludes rupture), S1 radiculopathy (lateral foot sensory loss + weak plantarflexion), Morton's neuroma (forefoot, 3rd/4th toes), calcaneal stress fracture.
Risk factors
Prolonged standing, running, obesity, poor footwear, tight calf/Achilles.
Diagnosis
CLINICAL; heel spur on X-ray is usually incidental (not the cause).
Management
Rest + supportive/cushioned footwear + insoles/heel pads + plantar/calf STRETCHING ± analgesia, night splints; self-limiting (~6–12 months); injection/shockwave/surgery if refractory.

Overview — lower back & spine
Causes of back pain ranging from benign mechanical pain to nerve-root, canal, infective and fracture pathology.
The organising principle: most back pain is mechanical and self-limiting — the skill is screening for red flags (cauda equina, malignancy, infection, fracture) and recognising radicular features.

What & why
Mechanical (non-specific) lower back pain = back pain from the muscles, ligaments, joints, or discs of the spine without a serious underlying cause — the commonest cause of back pain by far (>90%).
The core concept: the overwhelming majority of back pain is benign, self-limiting, "mechanical" — so the entire task is NOT to image everyone, but to screen for the RED FLAGS signalling a serious cause (cancer, infection, fracture, cauda equina). Most back pain needs only reassurance + analgesia + staying active; the red flags change the game. Imaging (MRI) is reserved for suspected serious pathology.

What the red flags point to: age >50 / previous cancer / night pain / weight loss → malignancy / metastatic spinal cord compression; fever / systemically unwell / IVDU → infection (discitis / epidural abscess); trauma / osteoporosis / steroids → vertebral fracture; saddle anaesthesia / bladder-bowel dysfunction / bilateral leg symptoms → cauda equina syndrome.
The cauda equina point: saddle anaesthesia + urinary retention/incontinence + faecal incontinence + bilateral sciatica = cauda equina syndrome → EMERGENCY MRI + decompression — the "must-never-miss".
Causes of mechanical back pain
  • Non-specific/mechanical — the commonest (muscle/ligament strain, poor posture, lifting).
  • Degenerative: facet joint osteoarthritis, degenerative disc disease, spondylosis.
  • Discogenic/radiculopathy: prolapsed intervertebral disc → sciatica.
  • Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication); spondylolisthesis (vertebral slippage).
The rule: most is non-specific/mechanical; consider disc prolapse (sciatica), stenosis, facet osteoarthritis — but always first exclude red flags.
Clinical features
  • Mechanical pattern: pain in the lower back (± buttock/thigh), worse with movement/certain postures, better with rest, no systemic features, no true morning stiffness.
  • Sciatica: pain radiating down the leg below the knee in a dermatomal pattern (± paraesthesia/weakness) — nerve root compression.
  • Assess: red flags, neurological exam (power, sensation, reflexes, straight leg raise), and cauda equina symptoms (saddle sensation, bladder/bowel).
The rule: mechanical = movement-related, no red flags, normal neurology; inflammatory back pain = morning stiffness, better with movement, young → think ankylosing spondylitis (not mechanical).
Investigations
  • Do NOT routinely image mechanical back pain — MRI only if indicated (red flags / suspected serious pathology, radiculopathy not settling, or before intervention). Routine X-rays/MRI are unhelpful (radiation, incidental findings).
  • Urgent MRI: suspected cauda equina, cord compression (malignancy), or infection.
  • Bloods if infection/malignancy suspected: FBC, CRP/ESR, ± myeloma screen / PSA.
The rule: red flags → investigate (MRI ± bloods); no red flags → NO imaging, treat conservatively.
Management

Principle: benign pain → reassurance + stay active + analgesia (NSAIDs); red-flag conditions → urgent referral / specific treatment.
  • Reassurance + education — most back pain is benign + self-limiting (good prognosis).
  • STAY ACTIVE + continue normal activities — avoid bed rest (worsens outcomes) — the cornerstone; exercise/physiotherapy for persistent pain.
  • 1st-line analgesia = NSAIDs (e.g. naproxen), co-prescribe a PPI in over-45s; short-term weak opioid (codeine) if NSAIDs insufficient/contraindicated.
  • NICE: do NOT routinely offer paracetamol alone, and avoid strong opioids, benzodiazepines, and gabapentinoids for low back pain.
The rule: reassure + stay active + NSAIDs (+PPI in over-45s) + physiotherapy for mechanical pain; avoid routine imaging, bed rest, paracetamol-alone and strong opioids; act urgently on red flags (cauda equina → emergency decompression; MSCC → dexamethasone + MRI + oncology; discitis → antibiotics).
Exam pearls
What it is
Benign, movement-related, self-limiting back pain (>90%); the key skill is screening for RED FLAGS.
RED FLAGS
Age <20 or >50, previous malignancy, night pain, trauma, systemically unwell (+ saddle anaesthesia / bladder-bowel → cauda equina).
Red flags point to
Malignancy/MSCC, infection (discitis/abscess), fracture, cauda equina (EMERGENCY).

Morning stiffness, better with movement, young → think ankylosing spondylitis (not mechanical).
Investigations
MRI ONLY if indicated (red flags) — don't routinely image simple back pain.
Management
Reassurance + STAY ACTIVE + NSAIDs (+PPI in over-45s) + physiotherapy; avoid bed rest, routine imaging, paracetamol-alone, strong opioids; urgent action on red flags.
What & why
Sciatica = leg pain from compression/irritation of a lumbosacral nerve root (radiculopathy), most often from a prolapsed (herniated) intervertebral disc — causing dermatomal leg pain with neurological deficits.
The core concept: a disc's nucleus pulposus herniates (usually posterolaterally, at L4/5 or L5/S1) → compresses the adjacent nerve root → pain, sensory change, weakness and reflex loss in that root's dermatome/myotome. So the picture is radicular (dermatomal) leg pain > back pain. Key skills: localise the level (dermatome/reflex/myotome), screen for cauda equina, and manage conservatively. Exam trap: sciatica is managed like ordinary back pain (NSAIDs) — not neuropathic agents.
  • Most sciatica is self-limiting; the "don't miss" is cauda equina syndrome.

The cauda equina fork: always screen — saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica, bilateral/severe leg weakness, reduced anal tone → EMERGENCY MRI + decompression.

  • Straight leg raise (SLR): passively raising the straight leg reproduces the radicular pain (stretches the root) → positive in L5/S1 radiculopathy.
The rule: dermatomal leg pain (worse than back pain, worse on sitting) + a neurological deficit + positive SLR = sciatica from a prolapsed disc.
Causes
  • Prolapsed (herniated) intervertebral disc — the commonest, typically at L4/5 or L5/S1.
  • Other: spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis (vertebral slippage), tumour (esp. metastasis), abscess, trauma.
The rule: the commonest cause of sciatica is a prolapsed disc (L4/5 or L5/S1); also stenosis, spondylolisthesis, tumour.
Investigations
  • A clinical diagnosis — the radicular pattern + neurological exam (dermatome, reflex, myotome, SLR).
  • Don't image early — MRI only if symptoms persist beyond ~4–6 weeks (most resolve), or urgently if red flags.
  • Urgent MRI: cauda equina symptoms → immediate.
The rule: clinical diagnosis; MRI if persists >4–6 weeks (or urgently for red flags) — don't image early.
Management
Principle: manage like ordinary mechanical back pain — analgesia (NSAIDs, NOT neuropathic agents) + stay active + physiotherapy; MRI/referral if persistent; surgery for refractory or red-flag cases.
  • Key NICE point: use the SAME drugs as for back pain without sciatica — 1st line = NSAIDs (± PPI) — NOT gabapentin/pregabalin/duloxetine (neuropathic agents are no longer recommended for sciatica).
  • Reassurance + stay active (avoid bed rest) + physiotherapy/exercise — most resolve within weeks.
  • Escalation: persistent/severe radicular pain → specialist referral; epidural corticosteroid injection, and surgery (microdiscectomy) for confirmed disc prolapse with persistent/severe symptoms or progressive deficit.
  • Progressive motor weakness or cauda equina → urgent surgery.
The rule: NSAIDs (+PPI) + stay active + physiotherapy → MRI + specialist referral if persisting beyond 4–6 weeks → epidural/surgery if refractory; urgent surgery for progressive deficit/cauda equina.

What & why
Lumbar spinal stenosis = narrowing of the central spinal canal (by degenerative change, disc prolapse, or tumour) → compressing the nerve roots/cauda equina → neurogenic claudication.
The core concept: the lumbar canal is progressively narrowed (usually by age-related degeneration — thickened ligamentum flavum, facet hypertrophy, bulging discs, osteophytes) → squeezing the nerve roots, worse when the canal narrows on standing/extension. The signature is neurogenic claudication: back + leg pain on walking/standing, relieved by sitting or bending forward (which opens the canal). The key skill is distinguishing this postural, canal-dependent pattern from vascular claudication. Clinical diagnosis confirmed on MRI; conservative first, decompressive laminectomy for refractory cases.
  • Typically older patients; the classic "shopping trolley sign" (leaning forward on a trolley relieves it).

  • Surgical: laminectomy — decompression (removing lamina ± ligamentum flavum/osteophytes to widen the canal) — for severe/refractory symptoms or significant neurological compromise.

What & why
Discitis = infection of the intervertebral disc space (often with adjacent vertebral involvement = spondylodiscitis / vertebral osteomyelitis) — which can lead to sepsis or an epidural abscess.
The core concept: bacteria seed the disc space (usually haematogenously, from a distant source) → local infection → severe back pain + systemic sepsis, and it can spread into the epidural space (abscess) → cord/nerve compression. Two threads dominate: (1) it's a "don't miss" — a septic patient with severe back pain ± new neurology needs MRI + blood cultures; and (2) because it's haematogenous, you must hunt for the ORIGIN — especially infective endocarditis. Treatment is prolonged IV antibiotics after identifying the organism.
  • Commonest organism: Staphylococcus aureus; a red-flag cause of back pain.

  • Treat the source + sepsis: ABCDE / sepsis six, treat endocarditis / the primary source if found; supportive care, spinal bracing as needed.
The rule: identify the organism → 6–8 weeks IV antibiotics; surgery for abscess/compression; find + treat the source (echo for endocarditis).

Osteoporotic vertebral fracture = a fragility fracture of a vertebral body — in osteoporosis there is an increased likelihood of fragility fractures, and the vertebrae are a very common site.
The core concept: the weakened vertebral body collapses under minimal load (a fragility fracture — low-energy trauma or even normal activity like bending/coughing). It typically wedges (crushes anteriorly) → the two hallmarks: acute back pain (though often silent/asymptomatic) and, cumulatively, progressive height loss + kyphosis. Priorities: recognise it (often incidental), exclude a sinister cause (malignancy — MRI to differentiate), and — crucially — treat the underlying osteoporosis to prevent the next fracture.
  • Often asymptomatic (found incidentally); a fragility fracture should always prompt osteoporosis assessment/treatment.

  • Treat the osteoporosis (the KEY step): calcium + vitamin D + a bisphosphonate and address risk factors — a fragility fracture is a strong indication for treatment to prevent the next one.
  • Vertebroplasty / kyphoplasty (cement injection) for severe, persistent pain not responding to conservative treatment.
  • Surgery for instability, neurological compromise (cord/cauda compression), or a pathological fracture; falls prevention + supportive back care.
The rule: analgesia + early mobilisation for the fracture; TREAT THE OSTEOPOROSIS (Ca/vit D + bisphosphonate) to prevent recurrence; vertebroplasty for refractory pain; surgery for instability/neurology.

Fragility fracture of a vertebral body (the commonest osteoporotic fracture); the vertebra wedges/collapses.

Often ASYMPTOMATIC; or acute back pain; cumulatively → height loss + thoracic KYPHOSIS + focal spinous-process tenderness; ± breathing/GI issues.
