ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint (Neuropathic:
What & why
Charcot joint (neuropathic arthropathy) = a progressive degeneration of a weight-bearing joint secondary to a LOSS OF SENSATION — the joint becomes badly disrupted and destroyed because the underlying neuropathy removes its protection.
The core concept: the whole disease flows from one idea — you protect your joints because they hurt. Lose the protective pain and proprioceptive sensation and the joint suffers repeated unnoticed micro-trauma → it progressively breaks down, fragments and dislocates, all while the patient feels relatively little pain (the paradox). The single most useful clue is that mismatch: a grossly swollen, warm, deformed, destroyed joint that hurts far LESS than it should. The commonest modern setting is the diabetic foot, and the key clinical challenge is distinguishing it from infection (osteomyelitis / cellulitis), which it closely mimics (both give a hot, swollen foot).
  • Insidious onset; commonest in the foot / ankle (diabetes).
  • A "don't miss" — early recognition and offloading can prevent catastrophic deformity.
The decisive fork: Charcot vs infection

The rule (high-yield): a hot, swollen, red foot that is relatively PAINLESS, with intact skin, that settles on elevation, in a diabetic = Charcot foot; fever, a skin break/ulcer and raised inflammatory markers point to infection — but the two can coexist.
The mismatch point: the hallmark is severe joint destruction with disproportionately little pain — the loss of sensation is exactly what makes it "not too painful".

  • MRI — for early disease (before X-ray changes) and to help distinguish Charcot from osteomyelitis (a key clinical difficulty).
  • Assess the underlying neuropathy — monofilament / vibration testing (confirm sensory loss), glucose / HbA1c.
  • Exclude infection — WCC / CRP, look for a wound / ulcer.
The rule (high-yield): X-ray = destruction, fragmentation, dislocation, remodelling → Charcot; MRI helps differentiate from osteomyelitis.
Management
Overarching principle: OFFLOAD the joint (immobilise / non-weight-bear) + treat the underlying neuropathy + protect the skin — a "don't miss, offload early" diagnosis.
Offloading — the key intervention
  • Immobilisation + non-weight-bearing — a total contact cast (or removable walker) to offload the affected joint during the acute (hot, active) phase → prevents further destruction / deformity.
  • Time-critical: early offloading preserves joint architecture; delay → progressive collapse and deformity.
Treat cause + protect the foot
  • Optimise glycaemic control (diabetes); manage the neuropathy; treat B12 deficiency / syphilis as relevant.
  • Diabetic foot MDT (podiatry, diabetology, orthotics), custom footwear / orthotics, regular foot care and ulcer prevention (the insensate destroyed foot is at high ulcer / amputation risk).
  • Bisphosphonates — sometimes used to reduce bone turnover (limited evidence).
  • Surgery — for severe deformity, instability or non-healing ulceration (reconstruction / arthrodesis; occasionally amputation).

Overview — dislocations
Traumatic displacement of a joint's articular surfaces — orthopaedic urgencies requiring prompt reduction and careful neurovascular assessment.
The organising principle: assess and document neurovascular status before and after reduction, image to confirm the direction and exclude associated fracture, and reduce promptly.

What & why
Shoulder (glenohumeral) dislocation = displacement of the humeral head out of the glenoid fossa — the most commonly dislocated major joint (the shoulder trades stability for its huge range of movement).
The core concept: the glenohumeral joint is a shallow ball-and-socket (large humeral head on a small, shallow glenoid) → highly mobile but inherently unstable → the commonest joint to dislocate. The key split is anterior vs posterior — different mechanisms, appearances and associations (anterior = FOOSH + axillary nerve injury; posterior = seizures/electric shock + easily missed). Priorities: assess neurovascular status (especially the axillary nerve) BEFORE and AFTER reduction, reduce it, and check a post-reduction X-ray.
  • Anterior is by far the commonest; the key "don't miss" is the axillary nerve injury and the easily-overlooked posterior dislocation.

  • Anterior: due to FOOSH → arm held in external rotation + abduction, loss of the rounded deltoid contour (squared shoulder), humeral head palpable anteriorly; severe pain + inability to move the arm.
  • Posterior: associated with seizures + electric shock/electrocution (violent internal-rotator contraction drives the head posteriorly); arm held adducted + internally rotated, resists external rotation.
The rule: FOOSH + externally rotated/abducted arm + squared shoulder = anterior; post-seizure/electric shock + internally rotated arm = posterior.
Neurovascular assessment: the axillary nerve

Anterior dislocation can cause an axillary nerve palsy: weak deltoid (weak shoulder abduction) + sensory loss over the "regimental badge" area (lateral deltoid).
  • Always assess neurovascular status — especially the axillary nerve — BEFORE and AFTER reduction (reduction itself can injure the nerve → pre- and post-reduction documentation is clinically and medicolegally essential).
  • Also assess the axillary artery (distal pulses/perfusion) and the wider brachial plexus.
The rule: sensory loss over the "regimental badge" area + weak deltoid = axillary nerve injury.
Investigations
  • X-ray before AND after reduction: pre-reduction confirms the dislocation + direction and any fracture-dislocation; post-reduction confirms relocation and no iatrogenic fracture.
  • Views: AP + lateral (scapular-Y) + axillary — the axillary/Y view is essential to detect a posterior dislocation (missed on AP alone).
  • Associated bony injuries: Hill-Sachs lesion (impaction fracture of the posterolateral humeral head) + Bankart lesion (anteroinferior glenoid labrum ± bone) — both predispose to recurrent dislocation.
The rule: X-ray before + after reduction (± axillary view for posterior); assess for Hill-Sachs / Bankart lesions.
Management
Principle: analgesia + prompt closed reduction (neurovascular checks before + after) → immobilise → rehabilitate; surgery for recurrent instability.
  • Reduction: if recent, may reduce with minimal sedation (e.g. Kocher technique); otherwise analgesia/sedation to relax the rotator cuff (muscle spasm prevents reduction). Techniques (Kocher, Hippocratic, Stimson, external rotation) all rely on relaxation + gentle, controlled reduction (avoid excessive force → fracture/nerve injury).
  • Post-reduction: re-assess neurovascular status + post-reduction X-ray; immobilise in a sling then physiotherapy to restore range and strengthen the rotator cuff/stabilisers.
  • Recurrent instability (esp. young patients, or with Bankart/Hill-Sachs lesions) → surgical stabilisation (e.g. Bankart repair).
Complications: axillary nerve injury, recurrent dislocation/instability, associated fractures (Hill-Sachs / Bankart / greater tuberosity), rotator cuff tear (esp. older patients), adhesive capsulitis.

What & why
Hip dislocation = displacement of the femoral head out of the acetabulum — a high-energy injury (most often a road traffic accident) and an orthopaedic emergency.
The core concept: the hip is a deep, stable ball-and-socket (unlike the shallow shoulder), so it takes major force to dislocate — hence high-energy trauma (the classic "dashboard injury") and frequent associated injuries. Two things make it time-critical: the femoral head's precarious retrograde blood supply (delayed reduction → avascular necrosis) and the posterior sciatic nerve (at risk in the common posterior dislocation). Priorities: ABCDE, assess the sciatic nerve, and reduce urgently (within ~6 hours, as soon as possible) to prevent avascular necrosis. Read the direction from the leg position.

Elbow dislocation = displacement of the ulna (± radius) from the distal humerus — the second most commonly dislocated major joint in adults (after the shoulder) and the commonest dislocation in children.

The common peroneal nerve is also frequently injured. The whole message: this is a vascular emergency — reduce urgently and obsessively assess/re-assess the popliteal artery (and peroneal nerve); a normal initial pulse does NOT exclude a limb-threatening arterial injury (it may thrombose later).

  • MRI later to define the ligamentous injury (for surgical planning).
The rule: X-ray + urgent vascular assessment (ABPI → CT angiography); MRI later for ligaments.

Principle: an emergency — URGENT reduction + obsessive vascular assessment; revascularise immediately if the artery is injured; then staged ligament reconstruction.
  • Immediate: ABCDE (high-energy trauma), analgesia; URGENT closed reduction (realigning the joint reduces vascular compromise) → re-assess neurovascular status + post-reduction X-ray; immobilise in a splint (knee slightly flexed).
  • Vascular (the priority): any arterial injury / absent pulses / ischaemia → emergency vascular surgery (revascularisation) — warm ischaemia time is limited (revascularise within ~6–8 hours). Even with normal pulses → serial observations + CT angiography. Watch for compartment syndrome (esp. after reperfusion).
  • Definitive: staged ligament reconstruction/repair once the limb is stable and vascular status secure; manage the common peroneal nerve injury (foot drop → ankle-foot orthosis; may recover or need later surgery).

What & why
Colles' and Smith's fractures are the two classic distal radius fractures — both ~1 inch (2.5 cm) proximal to the radiocarpal (wrist) joint — distinguished by the DIRECTION of displacement of the distal fragment.
The core concept: mirror-image fractures — the distinction is which way the wrist fragment tilts: Colles' = DORSAL displacement → "dinner fork" deformity; Smith's = VOLAR angulation → "reverse Colles' / garden spade". Mechanism gives it away: Colles' from a FOOSH (extended wrist) — the commonest — vs Smith's from a fall onto a FLEXED wrist. Priorities: recognise the deformity → confirm the direction on X-ray → assess the neurovascular status (especially the MEDIAN NERVE → acute carpal tunnel) → reduce/immobilise.
  • Colles' is by far the commonest — classically an osteoporotic post-menopausal woman after a fall (a fragility fracture).

"Colles' — Dorsally Displaced Distal radius → Dinner fork Deformity" (all the D's). The dorsally-displaced fragment gives the wrist the profile of an upturned dinner fork on the lateral view.
Colles' fracture
  • Pattern: transverse fracture of the radius, ~1 inch proximal to the radiocarpal joint (extra-articular).
  • Displacement: DORSAL displacement + angulation → dinner-fork deformity.
  • Mechanism: usually a FOOSH; the classic patient is an older, osteoporotic (post-menopausal) woman → a fragility fracture (assess/treat the osteoporosis).
The rule: FOOSH + a dinner-fork wrist deformity in an older woman = Colles' fracture.
Smith's fracture
  • VOLAR angulation of the distal fragment of an extra-articular distal radius fracture — the "reverse Colles'".
  • Mechanism: a fall onto a FLEXED wrist, or a blow to the dorsum of the wrist.
  • Smith's fractures are more UNSTABLE than Colles' (the volar tilt tends to displace) → more often need surgical fixation.
The rule: volar angulation (reverse Colles') from a flexed-wrist injury = Smith's fracture — more unstable, often surgical.
Clinical features & investigations
  • Features: wrist pain, swelling, deformity (dinner-fork or reverse), tenderness, reduced movement after a fall.
  • Assess neurovascular status — the median nerve especially + distal pulses/perfusion — before + after reduction.
  • X-ray (AP + lateral): confirms the fracture and the direction of displacement — the lateral view shows dorsal (Colles') vs volar (Smith's); assess intra- vs extra-articular + comminution.
The rule: wrist deformity + pain after a fall → assess the neurovascular status (median nerve) → X-ray (lateral shows dorsal vs volar).
Complications
TimingComplication
Earlymedian nerve injury → acute carpal tunnel syndrome; compartment syndrome; vascular compromise; malunion; rupture of the extensor pollicis longus (EPL) tendon

Acute carpal tunnel: the median nerve is at risk from the fracture/swelling → numbness/tingling in the median distribution → check for it. EPL rupture (often delayed) frays over the fracture callus → loss of thumb extension. CRPS is a late complication (disproportionate pain, swelling, skin/temperature changes).
Management
Principle: immobilise + refer; undisplaced → cast; displaced → closed reduction + cast; unstable/intra-articular → surgery; assess the median nerve + treat the osteoporosis.
  • Initial: immobilise (a Futuro splint or below-elbow backslab); refer to orthopaedics + repeat imaging in 7–10 days if the initial X-ray is inconclusive.
  • Undisplaced / minimally displaced → cast immobilisation (below-elbow).
  • Displaced → closed reduction (± regional anaesthesia / Bier's block) + cast; check post-reduction X-ray.
  • Unstable, intra-articular, or failed reduction → surgery — ORIF (volar plate) or K-wires / external fixation; Smith's often needs fixation.
  • Assess + manage the median nerve (acute carpal tunnel → may need urgent decompression); treat the osteoporosis + falls assessment.
The rule: immobilise + refer → undisplaced = cast; displaced = reduce + cast; unstable/intra-articular/Smith's = ORIF; check the median nerve; treat the osteoporosis.

What & why
Scaphoid fracture = a fracture of the scaphoid (the largest proximal-row carpal bone), often from a FOOSH → axial compression with the wrist hyperextended + radially deviated — the commonest carpal fracture.
The core concept: its importance comes from one fact — a RETROGRADE blood supply (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery, entering distally). Blood flows distal → proximal, so a fracture cuts off the proximal fragment → avascular necrosis (AVN) + non-union. This is the classic "don't miss" fracture: easily overlooked (often X-ray-occult early), and missing it → AVN, non-union, wrist arthritis. So the approach is defensive: anatomical snuffbox tenderness after a FOOSH → treat as a scaphoid fracture even if the X-ray is normal → immobilise + re-image. The more proximal the fracture, the worse the AVN risk.
  • Radial-sided wrist pain after a FOOSH; the key sign is anatomical snuffbox tenderness.
The decisive rule: treat it even if the X-ray is normal

Clinical features
FeatureDetail

The anatomical snuffbox = the hollow at the base of the thumb, bordered by the EPL tendon (ulnar side) and APL/EPB tendons (radial side), best seen on thumb extension; the scaphoid sits in its floor → tenderness here is the hallmark. Also tenderness over the scaphoid tubercle (palmar).
The rule: radial wrist pain after a FOOSH + anatomical snuffbox tenderness + pain on thumb telescoping = scaphoid fracture.
Investigations
  • X-ray — dedicated scaphoid views (AP, lateral, oblique + a scaphoid/ulnar-deviated view) — but may be NORMAL early (occult).
  • MRI = the definitive investigation — the most sensitive; detects an occult fracture not seen on X-ray (and assesses AVN).
  • Re-imaging pathway: if the initial X-ray is inconclusive but suspicion is high → immobilise + an early MRI (NICE NG38 — the preferred confirmatory test when the initial X-ray is normal), or repeat imaging in 7–10 days if MRI is unavailable.
The rule: X-ray (scaphoid views) → if normal but clinically suspected → immobilise + MRI (definitive) or repeat X-ray at 7–10 days — never discharge snuffbox tenderness on a single normal X-ray.
Management
Principle: immobilise ALL suspected/confirmed fractures (even with a normal X-ray) + refer; undisplaced → cast; displaced/proximal-pole/non-union → surgery; the goal is to prevent AVN + non-union.
  • Initial: immobilise a suspected/confirmed fracture (a Futuro splint or below-elbow backslab ± thumb spica); refer to orthopaedics + repeat imaging 7–10 days later if the X-ray is inconclusive.
  • Undisplaced → cast immobilisation (below-elbow, often 6–12 weeks — scaphoid fractures are slow to heal).
  • Displaced, proximal pole, or non-union → surgical fixation (a compression screw ± bone grafting for non-union/AVN) — the high-AVN-risk fractures.
  • Follow-up: monitor for union (may need CT); a non-union/AVN → surgery, and if untreated → SNAC wrist (scaphoid non-union advanced collapse) → arthritis.
The rule: immobilise all suspected fractures + refer; undisplaced → cast; displaced/proximal/non-union → surgery — to prevent AVN, non-union, and arthritis.

What & why
Galeazzi and Monteggia fractures are the two classic forearm FRACTURE-DISLOCATIONS — each = a fracture of ONE forearm bone PLUS a dislocation of ONE radioulnar joint (proximal or distal).
The core concept: the radius + ulna form a ring connected at both ends (the proximal + distal radioulnar joints) — so like any bony ring, if one bone fractures + displaces, a joint at the other end usually dislocates too. The lesson: when you see a single forearm-bone fracture, always look for the associated joint dislocation — the easily-missed dislocation causes long-term disability. Distinguished by which bone breaks + which joint dislocates (mnemonics GRUsome + MURder). Both usually need operative fixation in adults; the priority is prompt diagnosis.
  • Unifying rule: a forearm fracture → examine + X-ray BOTH the elbow AND the wrist → don't miss the dislocation.

  • Features: forearm pain, swelling, bruising, deformity, reduced/painful movement (esp. rotation) after a fall.
  • Examine + X-ray BOTH joints (elbow + wrist) — to catch the dislocation (the whole point).
  • Neurovascular status — esp. the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) in Monteggia (radial head dislocation) → check finger/thumb extension.

Principle: ORIF of the fractured bone in ADULTS (which reduces the dislocation) — closed reduction in CHILDREN — then immobilise; prompt diagnosis to avoid disability.

  • Monteggia: ORIF of the ulna (closed reduction in children) → reducing the ulna usually relocates the radial head → immobilise.
  • Adults → ORIF; children → often closed reduction (children's fractures remodel + the reduction holds better).
  • Monteggia needs prompt diagnosis — a missed radial head dislocation → chronic dislocation, deformity, and impaired forearm rotation.
The rule: fix the fractured bone (ORIF in adults / closed reduction in children) → this reduces the dislocation → immobilise; ensure the joint is reduced + stable.

What & why
Clavicle (collarbone) fracture = a fracture of the clavicle — one of the commonest fractures, typically from a fall onto the shoulder (or a FOOSH), across all ages.
The core concept: the clavicle is a subcutaneous S-shaped strut connecting the arm to the axial skeleton → it fractures easily and the deformity is often visible/palpable. The organising fact: ~80% fracture in the MIDDLE THIRD (thinnest, least supported), and most heal well conservatively (sling). Priorities: recognise the presentation (arm supported, head tilted toward the injury), assess the skin + neurovascular structures beneath (subclavian vessels + brachial plexus lie just deep), and identify the minority needing surgery.
  • The classic birth injury in a difficult delivery (shoulder dystocia).

Clinical features
  • Mechanism: a fall onto the shoulder (commonest), a FOOSH, or a direct blow; in neonates, birth trauma (shoulder dystocia).
  • Features: pain, swelling, a visible/palpable deformity/lump over the clavicle, bruising.
  • The patient supports the affected arm against the body and tilts the head toward the injured side (relaxing sternocleidomastoid/trapezius).
  • The medial fragment is pulled UP (by sternocleidomastoid); the lateral fragment DOWN + medially (arm weight + pectoralis).
The rule: fall onto the shoulder + pain/deformity over the collarbone + the arm supported against the body = clavicle fracture.
Assessment: the structures beneath
  • Skin: is it tented/threatened/broken (an open fracture)? → surgical urgency.
  • Neurovascular: the subclavian artery/vein + brachial plexus run just deep to the clavicle → check distal pulses/perfusion + limb neurology.
  • Associated injury: pneumothorax (esp. medial third/high-energy — the lung apex lies beneath), scapular/rib fractures, shoulder injury.
The rule: always check the skin (open/tented), the neurovascular status (subclavian vessels / brachial plexus), and for a pneumothorax.
Investigations
  • X-ray (AP ± cephalic tilt): confirms the fracture, the third involved, displacement, shortening, comminution.
  • CT — for medial-third fractures / suspected intra-thoracic or sternoclavicular injury.
  • CXR — if a pneumothorax is suspected (high-energy/medial).
The rule: X-ray classifies it (third, displacement); CT/CXR for medial-third or suspected chest injury.
Management
Principle: most (middle-third, minimally displaced) → conservative (sling + analgesia + early mobilisation); surgery for open/neurovascular/significantly displaced/lateral-third fractures.
  • Conservative (the majority): a broad arm sling (or collar-and-cuff) for comfort (~ a few weeks), analgesia, and early shoulder mobilisation (pendulum exercises) once comfortable → prevents stiffness. Most middle-third fractures unite well (accept some deformity/lump — often cosmetic).
  • Surgical — ORIF (plate) for: open fracture, threatened skin, neurovascular injury, significant displacement/shortening (>2 cm)/comminution, displaced lateral-third fractures, or non-union.
  • Neonatal fracture: heals rapidly with minimal/no intervention (gentle handling; good prognosis).
The rule: broad arm sling + analgesia + early mobilisation for most; ORIF for open/neurovascular/significantly displaced/lateral-third fractures. Complications: non-union/malunion (esp. displaced/lateral-third), persistent lump, neurovascular injury, rarely pneumothorax.

What & why
Radial head fracture = a fracture of the head of the radius (at the elbow) — the commonest elbow fracture in ADULTS, typically from a FOOSH.
The core concept: on a FOOSH, axial load drives the radial head into the capitellum → fracturing it. Two things organise the topic: (1) the effect on FOREARM ROTATION — the radial head is central to supination/pronation, so restoring painless rotation is the goal and a mechanical block to rotation is a major surgical indication; and (2) associated injuries — the same force can damage the elbow ligaments, the coronoid (the "terrible triad"), and the DRUJ/interosseous membrane (an Essex-Lopresti injury). Most are undisplaced → conservative + EARLY mobilisation (the elbow stiffens easily). The classic clue is a positive fat pad sign on X-ray.
  • Lateral elbow pain + painful/restricted forearm rotation after a FOOSH; assess rotation + for a mechanical block.

A block to forearm rotation is a key surgical indication (aspirating the haemarthrosis + injecting local anaesthetic helps assess whether the block is mechanical vs just painful).
Clinical features
  • Mechanism: FOOSH — axial load driving the radial head into the capitellum.
  • Features: lateral elbow pain + tenderness over the radial head, swelling, an elbow effusion (haemarthrosis); painful + restricted forearm ROTATION (supination/pronation) — the key functional sign; reduced/painful flexion-extension.
  • Assess: a mechanical block to rotation? (surgical indication); neurovascular status (posterior interosseous nerve); and the whole forearm + wrist for an Essex-Lopresti injury (radial head fracture + interosseous membrane disruption + DRUJ dislocation → wrist pain).
The rule: FOOSH + lateral elbow pain + painful/restricted forearm rotation = radial head fracture → test for a mechanical block + check the wrist (Essex-Lopresti).
Investigations
  • X-ray (AP + lateral): shows the fracture + displacement, and the FAT pad sign — an effusion pushes the fat pads out: an anterior "sail sign", and importantly ANY posterior fat pad is abnormal → an intra-articular fracture (often the only sign of an occult, undisplaced radial head fracture).
  • CT — for comminuted fractures / surgical planning.
  • Assess the wrist/DRUJ if Essex-Lopresti is suspected.
The rule: X-ray — look for the fracture AND the fat pad sign (a posterior fat pad = occult fracture until proven otherwise); CT for comminution.
Management
Principle: undisplaced (Mason I) → conservative with EARLY mobilisation; displaced with a mechanical block (Mason II) → ORIF; comminuted (Mason III) → fixation or replacement; treat associated injuries.
  • Conservative (Mason I): a sling/collar-and-cuff briefly for comfort, then EARLY active mobilisation (within days) — the elbow is very prone to stiffness; analgesia ± aspiration of a tense haemarthrosis.
  • Mason II (displaced, mechanical block) → ORIF (screws/plate).
  • Mason III (comminuted, unreconstructable) → radial head EXCISION or REPLACEMENT (replacement preferred if the elbow is unstable — the radial head is a key stabiliser).
  • Mason IV / terrible triad → surgery (fix/replace radial head + repair coronoid + ligaments + reduce the dislocation).
The rule: undisplaced → sling + EARLY mobilisation (avoid stiffness); displaced/block → ORIF; comminuted → excision/replacement; associated dislocation/ligament injury → surgery.
Complications
  • Elbow STIFFNESS / loss of extension (the commonest — hence early mobilisation), post-traumatic osteoarthritis, instability (esp. with associated ligament injury — the radial head is a key stabiliser), a missed Essex-Lopresti (chronic wrist pain/DRUJ instability), posterior interosseous nerve injury.
The rule: the key complications are stiffness (mobilise early) and instability / missed associated injury (assess the ligaments + wrist).

What & why
Neck of femur (hip) fracture = a fracture of the proximal femur — one of the most common + important orthopaedic injuries, especially in the elderly (a fragility fracture).
The core concept: the whole management hinges on ONE anatomical fact — the femoral head has a RETROGRADE blood supply (up the neck from below). So the decisive question is: does the fracture disrupt that blood supply? — i.e. is it intracapsular (threatens the head → AVN risk → REPLACE) or extracapsular (blood supply intact → FIX). Everything (Garden classification, displaced-vs-undisplaced, implant choice) flows from this. It presents unmistakably (shortened + externally rotated leg) and, as a fragility fracture, mandates osteoporosis treatment + falls assessment.
  • Classic sign: a shortened + externally rotated leg + hip pain; a fragility fracture in the elderly.

  • The classic sign: a SHORTENED + EXTERNALLY ROTATED leg — from the pull of muscles on the displaced distal fragment (± abducted); ± inability to straight-leg raise.
  • Context: usually a low-energy fall in an elderly (osteoporotic) patient (a fragility fracture); in the young, it takes high-energy trauma.
The rule: elderly patient + fall + hip/groin pain + shortened, externally rotated leg = hip fracture.
Investigations
  • X-ray (AP + lateral): shows the fracture; an intracapsular fracture disrupts Shenton's line (a smooth curve along the inferior femoral neck + superior pubic ramus — a break indicates a fracture).
  • MRI (or CT): if the X-ray is normal but a fracture is clinically suspected (an occult fracture) — MRI is the most sensitive.
  • Pre-operative workup: bloods, ECG, group & save, fitness for anaesthesia; assess/treat the osteoporosis (DEXA) + a falls assessment.
The rule: X-ray (disrupted Shenton's line) → MRI if occult; pre-op workup + osteoporosis/falls assessment.
Management
Principle: surgery for almost all (early — within 36–48h); operation chosen by intracapsular-vs-extracapsular + displaced-vs-undisplaced (driven by AVN risk); + analgesia + treat the osteoporosis.

Intracapsular displaced → THR (fit/mobile/cognitively intact) or hemiarthroplasty (frailer); extracapsular stable → DHS; unstable/subtrochanteric → intramedullary nail.

Early surgery, analgesia, orthogeriatrics, treat the osteoporosis + falls assessment.
What & why
Patellar fracture = a fracture of the patella (kneecap) — the sesamoid within the quadriceps/patellar tendon that acts as the fulcrum for knee extension.
The core concept: the patella is the linchpin of the extensor mechanism (quadriceps → patella → patellar tendon → tibial tuberosity), so the single most important question is: is the extensor mechanism intact? — i.e. can the patient straight-leg raise / actively extend the knee? This one test drives everything: intact + undisplaced → conservative (brace); disrupted or displaced → surgery. The mechanism predicts the pattern: a direct blow → undisplaced/comminuted with the mechanism intact; an indirect (violent quadriceps contraction) → a transverse fracture that pulls apart → disrupts the extensor mechanism.
  • Presents with anterior knee pain/swelling after trauma; the key assessment is active knee extension / straight-leg raise.

The rule: direct blow → undisplaced/comminuted, mechanism usually intact; indirect (violent quads contraction) → transverse fracture that can DISRUPT the extensor mechanism. The critical question — is the extensor mechanism intact? (active knee extension / straight-leg raise) — decides conservative vs surgical management.
Clinical features
  • Swelling + bruising around the knee; pain + tenderness localised to the knee/patella.
  • A palpable gap/defect over the patella (in a displaced transverse fracture); a haemarthrosis.
The rule: anterior knee pain, swelling, bruising + tenderness over the patella after trauma = patellar fracture → assess the extensor mechanism.
Assessing the extensor mechanism
"Able to straight-leg raise?" = intact extensor mechanism. If the patient CAN actively extend the knee / straight-leg raise → the mechanism is INTACT; if they CANNOT → it is DISRUPTED (needs surgery).
  • Technique tip: better to test on the patient's SIDE to eliminate gravity — removing gravity's resistance means pain doesn't cause a false "can't lift".
The rule: the ability to actively extend the knee / straight-leg raise = an intact extensor mechanism → this single finding decides conservative vs surgical management.
Investigations
  • Plain X-ray — AP + lateral: confirms the fracture + assesses displacement + pattern (transverse/comminuted); the lateral view best shows displacement.
  • Beware the bipartite patella — a normal variant (a smooth, superolateral separate ossicle; often bilateral, smooth margins) — don't mistake it for a fracture.
The rule: AP + lateral X-ray (assess displacement/pattern); distinguish from a bipartite patella.
Management
Principle: intact extensor mechanism + undisplaced → conservative (hinged knee brace); disrupted mechanism or displaced → surgical fixation.

Undisplaced + intact extensor mechanismNO surgery → a hinged knee brace for 6 weeks; the patient can FULLY weight-bear
Displaced OR loss of the extensor mechanismoperation — tension band wire, inter-fragment screws, or cerclage wires → hinged brace for 4–6 weeks
Tension band wiring is the classic fixation for a transverse patellar fracture — it converts the distracting tensile forces of the quadriceps into compressive forces across the fracture. Supportive: analgesia, physiotherapy (regain quads strength + range), early mobilisation in the brace. Rare (severe comminution): partial/total patellectomy.

Fracture of the kneecap (a sesamoid in the extensor mechanism).

Is the EXTENSOR MECHANISM intact? — test by active knee extension / straight-leg raise (do it on the SIDE to eliminate gravity so pain doesn't cause a false failure).

Intact + undisplaced → hinged knee brace 6 weeks (full weight-bearing); displaced or mechanism lost → surgery (tension band wire / screws / cerclage) → hinged brace 4–6 weeks.

Tension band wire for a transverse fracture (converts tension into compression).
What & why
Ankle fracture = a fracture of the malleoli (± the distal tibia/fibula) around the ankle joint — one of the commonest lower-limb fractures, usually from a twisting/inversion injury.
The core concept: the ankle is a "mortise" — a socket of distal tibia + medial malleolus + lateral malleolus (fibula), held by the syndesmosis. Mortise stability is everything, so two questions organise it: (1) is it fractured? (use the Ottawa ankle rules to decide who needs an X-ray), and (2) is it STABLE? (the Weber classification asks where the fibular fracture sits relative to the syndesmosis). This drives management: stable → conservative (boot); unstable → surgery (ORIF). Two safety imperatives: promptly reduce a deformed/dislocated ankle to protect the skin, and don't delay reduction for an X-ray if there's neurovascular compromise.
  • The flow: Ottawa (do I image?) → Weber (is it stable?) → treat.

  • Mechanism: usually a twisting/inversion (or eversion) injury.
  • Features: pain, swelling, bruising, deformity, inability to weight-bear, malleolar tenderness.
  • Assess: the skin (tented/threatened — a deformed/dislocated ankle risks necrosis → prompt reduction); neurovascular status (pulses, sensation, capillary refill, before + after reduction); and the whole fibula (a proximal fibular fracture + syndesmosis injury = a Maisonneuve fracture).
The rule: assess the skin + neurovascular status; a deformed/dislocated ankle needs prompt reduction.
Investigations
  • X-ray (per Ottawa): AP, lateral + mortise views — assess the fracture, the Weber type, and mortise congruity / syndesmosis.
  • Weber B needs a radiograph to check the syndesmosis + mortise for stability (± stress/weight-bearing views).
  • CT for complex/comminuted fractures or surgical planning.
Critical safety rule: do NOT delay for an X-ray in an obvious ankle injury with neurovascular compromise → REDUCE FIRST.
Management
Prompt reduction FIRST: ALL ankle fractures should be promptly reduced (closed reduction is the most immediate management) to remove pressure on the overlying skin + prevent necrosis.

The rule: reduce all promptly → Weber A stable → CAM boot; Weber B → check stability (stable = boot, unstable = surgery); Weber C unstable → ORIF.

Malleolar fracture; stability of the ankle MORTISE (tibia + medial + lateral malleolus + syndesmosis) is everything.

AP/lateral/mortise views; CT for complex fractures.
What & why
Metatarsal fractures = fractures of the long bones of the forefoot — the commonest foot fractures, with the 5th metatarsal most commonly fractured and the 2nd metatarsal the classic stress-fracture site.
The core concept: two patterns dominate. First, the 5th metatarsal base — where the critical distinction is a proximal avulsion (pseudo-Jones) vs a true Jones fracture, because they sit in different zones with different blood supplies/healing (the Jones fracture is at a watershed zone → poor healing/non-union risk). Second, the stress fracture — a fatigue fracture from repetitive loading in athletes, classically the 2nd metatarsal shaft, often invisible on early X-ray. Two organising questions: which metatarsal + where (5th base: pseudo-Jones vs Jones)? and acute vs stress fracture?
  • Presents with forefoot pain, bony tenderness, swelling, an antalgic gait; the 5th metatarsal fracture classically follows an inversion ankle injury.

  • 5th metatarsal: often a history of an inversion ankle injury; tenderness over the base of the 5th metatarsal.

The rule: forefoot pain + bony tenderness + swelling + antalgic gait = metatarsal fracture; inversion injury → 5th base; insidious athlete's forefoot pain → 2nd metatarsal stress fracture.
Investigations
  • X-ray (AP, lateral, oblique): differentiate displaced from non-displaced; shows the acute fracture (e.g. a Jones fracture).
  • Stress fractures: X-ray often NORMAL early → use an isotope bone scan OR MRI (MRI most sensitive; bone scan shows increased uptake); a repeat X-ray at ~2 weeks may show healing callus.
  • Apply the Ottawa foot rules (midfoot-zone pain + tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal/navicular, or inability to weight-bear).
The rule: X-ray first (displaced vs non-displaced; shows acute fractures); for a suspected stress fracture with a normal X-ray → MRI or bone scan.
Management
Principle: most are conservative (supportive footwear/cast, weight-bear as tolerated); a Jones fracture + displaced/multiple fractures need closer follow-up ± surgery; stress fractures need REST + graded return.
  • Most (undisplaced) → conservative: stiff-soled footwear or a walking boot/cast, weight-bear as tolerated, analgesia, elevation.
  • 5th metatarsal — pseudo-Jones (avulsion) → usually conservative (supportive footwear/boot, weight-bear as tolerated).
  • 5th metatarsal — Jones fracture → more cautious: immobilisation + non-weight-bearing, closer follow-up (higher non-union risk); surgical fixation (screw) considered, esp. in athletes or if it fails to unite.
  • Stress fractures → REST + activity modification, gradual/graded return; treat any underlying cause (training errors, biomechanics, low bone density/energy availability).
  • Displaced/multiple/unstable → reduction ± surgical fixation (ORIF/K-wires).
The rule: undisplaced → conservative (boot, weight-bear as tolerated); Jones fracture → cautious ± surgery (non-union risk); stress fracture → rest + graded return; displaced/multiple → fixation.

Undisplaced → supportive footwear/boot, weight-bear as tolerated; Jones → cautious ± surgical screw; stress → rest + graded return; displaced/multiple → fixation.
What & why
Tibial plateau fracture = a fracture of the proximal tibial articular surface (the plateau) — the weight-bearing top of the tibia that forms the lower half of the knee joint.
The core concept: an intra-articular, weight-bearing surface, so it matters for two reasons: (1) joint congruity — any step-off/depression predisposes to post-traumatic osteoarthritis (restore a smooth surface); and (2) associated soft-tissue + neurovascular injury — the mechanism (axial load ± valgus/varus) frequently damages ligaments, menisci, the popliteal artery, and common peroneal nerve, and swelling risks compartment syndrome. Classic mechanism: high-energy axial load (fall from height, road traffic accident / "bumper injury") or a low-energy fall in the osteoporotic elderly. The lateral plateau is most commonly fractured. Assessment centres on neurovascular status + compartment syndrome; management on restoring the articular surface.
  • Painful, swollen knee + can't weight-bear; a haemarthrosis with fat globules (lipohaemarthrosis) signals an intra-articular fracture.

  • Mechanism: axial load ± valgus/varus force to the knee.
  • Features: painful, swollen knee (often a large haemarthrosis), inability to weight-bear, restricted movement, ± deformity.
  • Lipohaemarthrosis: aspirating blood with fat globules (or a fat-fluid level on imaging) indicates an intra-articular fracture (marrow fat leaks into the joint).
  • Assess: neurovascular status (popliteal artery, peroneal nerve), compartment syndrome, skin (open fracture?), associated ligament/meniscal injury.
The rule: painful swollen knee + can't weight-bear after axial trauma + a tense haemarthrosis = tibial plateau fracture → assess neurovascular status + compartment syndrome.
Investigations
  • X-ray (AP + lateral) — first-line: shows the fracture, articular depression/split, and a lipohaemarthrosis (fat-fluid level).
  • CT — the key investigation: defines the articular surface (depression/step-off + comminution) for surgical planning — essential for most plateau fractures.
  • MRI for associated ligament + meniscal injuries (± occult fractures); CT angiography if vascular injury suspected (esp. dislocation component).
The rule: X-ray → CT (define the articular surface, plan surgery) → MRI for soft tissues.

Management
Principle: restore the articular surface + knee alignment/stability; undisplaced → conservative; displaced/depressed intra-articular → ORIF; manage the associated emergencies first.

  • Non-operative (undisplaced/minimal depression, stable): hinged knee brace + protected/non-weight-bearing, then graded weight-bearing + physiotherapy.
  • Operative: displaced, depressed articular surface, or unstable → ORIF — elevate the depressed fragment, bone graft the defect, stabilise with plates/screws to restore a congruent joint surface.
  • Associated injuries: compartment syndrome → fasciotomy; vascular injury → revascularisation; ligament/meniscal repair as needed.
The rule: undisplaced → brace + non-weight-bearing; displaced/depressed intra-articular → ORIF (restore the joint surface, bone graft, plate/screws); treat compartment syndrome/vascular injury urgently.
Complications
  • Post-traumatic osteoarthritis — the commonest long-term (from articular incongruity).
  • Compartment syndrome, neurovascular injury (popliteal artery, peroneal nerve).
  • Knee stiffness/instability, malunion/non-union, infection (esp. open/operative).
The rule: the key long-term complication is post-traumatic osteoarthritis (hence restoring the joint surface); the key acute ones are compartment syndrome + neurovascular injury.

What & why
Buckle (torus) fracture = an incomplete paediatric fracture from a COMPRESSION force, creating a "buckle" as if the bone was shortened — a compression buckling of one cortex (the cortex crumples/bulges rather than breaking through).
The core concept: children's bones are soft, elastic, and have a thick periosteum — so rather than snapping, they bend, buckle and bow. A buckle fracture is the archetype: an axial/compression force (a fall on an outstretched hand) crumples one side of the soft cortex — like compressing a drinks can — without a true break through the bone. This makes it an inherently STABLE, benign fracture that heals readily. Two threads: recognise it as stable + benign (splint/removable brace), and — as with any paediatric fracture — consider safeguarding if the story doesn't fit.
  • Very common (classically the distal radius after a FOOSH); part of the incomplete-paediatric-fracture family (with greenstick).

Clinical features
  • Mechanism: a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) or axial load — classically a distal radius (wrist) buckle fracture.
  • Features: localised pain, tenderness, and swelling over the site; usually minimal/no deformity (it's incomplete + stable), often still able to use the limb.
The rule: a child + a FOOSH + localised wrist/forearm pain + tenderness + swelling, but no gross deformity = likely a buckle fracture.
Investigations
  • X-ray (2 views): a subtle "buckling"/bulging of the cortex (an outward bump) without a lucent fracture line through the bone.
  • Buckle fractures are easy to miss — look carefully for a cortical bulge/angulation (compare with the opposite side if needed).
The rule: X-ray shows a cortical bulge (buckle) without a complete break — look carefully, it's subtle.
Management
Principle: stable + benign → simple immobilisation (splint/removable brace) + heals readily; consider safeguarding.
  • Because it's stable + benign, current practice favours a removable splint / wrist brace (rather than a full plaster cast) for ~3 weeks — equally effective, more comfortable, and often doesn't require fracture-clinic follow-up.
  • Analgesia; heals reliably with an excellent prognosis (children heal fast + remodel well).
Safeguarding (ALL paediatric fractures): does the mechanism fit the injury + the child's developmental stage? Non-accidental-injury red flags — an inconsistent/changing history, delayed presentation, a non-ambulant child, or multiple fractures of different ages → escalate per safeguarding pathways.
A note on greenstick fractures
  • A greenstick fracture = a unilateral cortical breach only — an incomplete fracture, usually at the shaft of a long bone, from a bending mechanism.
  • Like bending a green (living) twig — it cracks on the outer (tension) side but the inner (compression) cortex stays intact.
  • Management: consider safeguarding + immobilisation in a cast; angulated greenstick fractures may need reduction (± completing the intact cortex to correct alignment).
The contrast: buckle = compression → a bulge (both cortices intact, just buckled); greenstick = bending → one cortex breaks (unilateral breach).

The result is a relatively stable, incomplete fracture with an intact cortex/periosteum on one side that aids healing and reduction. Two threads: recognise the incomplete pattern (correct any angulation), and consider safeguarding.

What & why
Salter-Harris fractures = fractures involving the GROWTH PLATE (physis) in children — classified I–V by the fracture pattern relative to the physis.
The core concept: children have an open growth plate (physis) — a cartilaginous zone of weakness between the epiphysis (the end, near the joint) and the metaphysis (the flared shaft). Because cartilage is weaker than bone and ligament, force often propagates through the physis rather than tearing a ligament (a child fractures the growth plate more than "sprains"). The classification describes which structures the fracture involves — and this matters because damage to the physis can arrest growth → limb-length discrepancy or angular deformity. The organising rule is the SALTER mnemonic, and the principle is that higher types (III–V) more likely disturb growth + involve the joint → worse prognosis.
  • Exclusively paediatric (only while the physis is open); the higher the number, generally the worse the outlook.

The rule: Type II is the COMMONEST (~75%); Types III + IV cross into the epiphysis → they are INTRA-ARTICULAR (involve the joint surface) → higher risk of joint incongruity + growth disturbance → often need anatomical reduction/fixation.
Clinical features
  • A child with pain, tenderness, and swelling over a joint/physeal region after trauma; point tenderness over the growth plate.
The rule: in a child, tenderness localised over the growth plate after injury = suspect a Salter-Harris fracture (even if the X-ray looks normal — a Salter-Harris I can be radiographically occult).
Investigations
  • X-ray (2 views) — the primary investigation; assess the physis + fracture pattern (which structures are involved → the type).
  • Types I + V can be radiographically NORMAL / subtle (the fracture is through cartilage) → clinical diagnosis on physeal tenderness; Type V (crush) is often only diagnosed retrospectively when growth arrest appears.
  • Compare with the other side if unsure; MRI/CT for complex intra-articular (III/IV) fractures or surgical planning.
The rule: X-ray classifies the type; but types I + V may look normal → treat on clinical suspicion (physeal tenderness).
Management & prognosis
Principle: lower types (I–II) → usually closed reduction + immobilisation; intra-articular types (III–IV) → often anatomical reduction ± fixation; the higher the type, the greater the growth-arrest risk.
  • Types I–II (extra-articular): usually closed reduction + cast immobilisation → generally heal well with a good prognosis (growth usually preserved).
  • Types III–IV (intra-articular): often require anatomical (open) reduction + internal fixation to restore the joint surface + physis alignment → higher risk of growth disturbance.
  • Type V (crush): poor prognosis — the physis is crushed → high risk of growth arrest (often diagnosed only when deformity/shortening appears).
Key complications: growth arrest → limb-length discrepancy (whole physis) or angular deformity (partial/asymmetric arrest); joint incongruity → post-traumatic osteoarthritis (intra-articular types). Children with physeal fractures need follow-up to monitor for growth disturbance.
The prognosis rule: the HIGHER the Salter-Harris type, the WORSE the prognosis — I–II good; III–IV guarded (intra-articular); V worst (crush).
Exam pearls
What it is
Fractures involving the GROWTH PLATE (physis) in children; the physis is a cartilaginous zone of weakness → fractures propagate through it (rather than a ligament tearing).
SALTER mnemonic
Slipped (I, physis only) · Above (II, + metaphysis — COMMONEST) · Lower (III, + epiphysis — intra-articular) · Through Everything (IV, all 3 — intra-articular) · Rammed (V, crush).
Intra-articular = III + IV
Cross the epiphysis → joint surface → anatomical reduction/fixation.
Occult types
Types I + V can look NORMAL on X-ray → suspect on physeal tenderness; Type V often diagnosed retrospectively (growth arrest).
Management
I–II → closed reduction + cast (good prognosis); III–IV → often ORIF (intra-articular); V → poor (growth arrest).
Key complication
GROWTH ARREST → limb-length discrepancy / angular deformity → the higher the type, the worse the prognosis; follow up for growth disturbance.
